dailies.passageText: 36 “Teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the Law?” 37 Jesus replied: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’ 40 All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments.”

weeks.planTitle: Grace: Jesus paid for our sin
weeks.title: Grace: Jesus paid for our sin
weeks.selectLabel: Week 13 · Grace: Jesus paid for our sin
weeks.nextUp: Week 14 · Faith and repentance (the lost son)
weeks.bigIdea: We were dead in our sins and could not save ourselves, but God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ. Jesus paid for our sin. Salvation is a gift of grace through faith, not something we earn.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 13 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Ephesians 2:1–10 out loud, then Romans 5:6–11 and Isaiah 53:4–6.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 1 As for you, you were dead in your transgressions and sins, 2 in which you used to live when you followed the ways of this world and of the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient. 3 All of us also lived among them at one time, gratifying the cravings of our flesh and following its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature deserving of wrath. 4 But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, 5 made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions—it is by grace you have been saved. 6 And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus, 7 in order that in the coming ages he might show the incomparable riches of his grace, expressed in his kindness to us in Christ Jesus. 8 For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God— 9 not by works, so that no one can boast. 10 For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.

6 You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. 7 Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. 8 But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 9 Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him! 10 For if, while we were God’s enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life! 11 Not only is this so, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

4 Surely he took up our pain and bore our suffering, yet we considered him punished by God, stricken by him, and afflicted. 5 But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed. 6 We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.

story: Last week we learned that God gave good commands to show us how to love him and love others, and that his law is like a mirror. It shows us that we have all sinned in our hearts, our words, and our actions, and that we need his help and forgiveness. This week we ask: what has God done about our sin?

Paul writes to the church in Ephesus and tells the truth first: we were dead in our transgressions and sins. Dead people cannot climb out and save themselves. But God is rich in mercy. Because of his great love, he made us alive with Christ. Paul says it plainly: it is by grace you have been saved, through faith — and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast.

Romans 5 shows us the same love in Jesus himself. “God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” He did not wait until we got ourselves cleaned up. He came for us when we were powerless.

Long before Jesus was born, Isaiah spoke of a servant who would take our place: “he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” “We all, like sheep, have gone astray… and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Jesus paid for our sin. That is grace: a gift we did not earn, given because God loves us.

Grace does not mean our sin does not matter. It means Jesus has paid for it, and everyone who trusts him is made alive with him. Then we get to do the good works God prepared for us — not to buy his love, but because we already have it as a gift.
weeks.enochLine: Jesus paid for my sin! God gives me a gift I cannot earn!
enochActivities: Activity: The free gift. Place a small wrapped gift on the table. Let Enoch hold it and say, “I didn’t earn this. It’s a gift!” Then say together, “Jesus paid for my sin. God’s love is a gift!”
Activity: Cross and heart. Draw a simple cross and a heart. Point to the cross and say, “Jesus paid.” Point to the heart and say, “God loves me!”
elijahQuestions: In Ephesians 2:8, how are we saved?
In Ephesians 2:9, why is this “not by works”?
In Romans 5:8, when did Christ die for us?
In Isaiah 53:6, what has the LORD laid on him?
jordynQuestions: Ephesians 2:1–5 says we were dead in our sins, and then God made us alive with Christ. Why does it matter that Paul calls us “dead,” not just “in trouble”?
Ephesians 2:8–10 says we are not saved by works, and then says we are created in Christ Jesus to do good works. If works cannot save us, what are those good works for?
Isaiah 53:5–6 and Romans 5:8 together: who did Jesus die for, and how should that change the way you treat someone who feels too far gone, or someone who has wronged you?
weeks.jordynApplication: Grace is a gift you cannot earn (Ephesians 2:8–9). This week, when you are tempted to think God will love you more if you perform, or to look down on someone who has failed, stop and say Ephesians 2:8 out loud. Then do one quiet kindness for someone who cannot pay you back.
elijahAnswers: “By grace… through faith… it is the gift of God” (Ephesians 2:8).
So that no one can boast (Ephesians 2:9). We cannot take credit for saving ourselves.
“While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).
“The iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6).
jordynAnswers: Dead people cannot save themselves (Ephesians 2:1, 5). We needed God, who is rich in mercy, to make us alive with Christ because of his great love — not a little help, but new life.

We are not saved by works, but we are “created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do” (Ephesians 2:10). The good works are the fruit of a gift already given, not a way to earn the gift.

Jesus died for sinners — for people who had gone astray like sheep (Isaiah 53:6; Romans 5:8). No one is too far gone for his grace, and we do not get to treat others as if they must earn what we received as a gift.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she stopped to say Ephesians 2:8, and how the quiet kindness went. Share one place you needed grace this week too, and pray for each other.
weeks.prayer: Dear God, thank you that you are rich in mercy and that you made us alive with Christ. Thank you that Jesus died for us while we were still sinners, and that he paid for our sin. Thank you that salvation is your gift, not something we earn. Help us trust you, and help us do the good works you prepared for us with grateful hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: We were dead in our sins, but God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ. That is grace.
dailies.verse: But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions—it is by grace you have been saved.
dailies.enoch: Say with a parent, “I was in trouble, but God loves me and made me alive with Jesus!”
dailies.elijah: In Ephesians 2:1, what were we in our transgressions and sins?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Dead” (verse 1).
dailies.jordyn: Paul says we were “dead,” not only weak. What does that tell you about trying to save yourself by being better?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Dead people cannot save themselves (verses 1, 5). Being better cannot raise the dead. We needed God to make us alive with Christ by grace.
dailies.action: Read Ephesians 2:4–5 together twice. Then each person thanks God for one way he has been rich in mercy to your family.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you are rich in mercy and that you made us alive with Christ. We could not save ourselves. Thank you for your great love and your grace. Help us remember it today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we learned that Jesus paid for our sin, and that salvation is a gift. Paul begins with hard news: we were dead in our transgressions and sins. We followed the ways of this world, and like the rest we were by nature deserving of wrath. Dead people cannot climb out and save themselves. Then come the best two words in the passage: “But… God.” Because of his great love, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ even when we were dead. Paul will not let us miss the point: it is by grace you have been saved. Grace means God did for us what we could not do for ourselves.
dailies.enochActivity: Lie down like you are “asleep,” then have a parent take your hand and help you stand up. Say, “God made me alive with Jesus!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verses 4–5, why did God make us alive with Christ?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Because of his great love for us,” and he “is rich in mercy” (verses 4–5). “It is by grace you have been saved.”
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 3 says “all of us” lived this way “at one time.” How should that keep you from looking down on someone who is still far from God?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We were in the same place (verse 3). Grace leaves no room to boast. We can tell the truth about sin and still remember that God is rich in mercy toward people like us.
dailies.passageText: 1 As for you, you were dead in your transgressions and sins, 2 in which you used to live when you followed the ways of this world and of the ruler of the kingdom of the air, the spirit who is now at work in those who are disobedient. 3 All of us also lived among them at one time, gratifying the cravings of our flesh and following its desires and thoughts. Like the rest, we were by nature deserving of wrath. 4 But because of his great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, 5 made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in transgressions—it is by grace you have been saved.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: Salvation is a gift of grace through faith, not a prize we earn. Then we get to do the good works God already prepared for us.
dailies.verse: For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God—not by works, so that no one can boast.
dailies.enoch: Hold out two empty hands and say, “I can’t buy this. It’s God’s gift!”
dailies.elijah: In Ephesians 2:8, what is salvation called?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “The gift of God” (verse 8).
dailies.jordyn: If someone said, “I will be good enough this week so God will love me,” how would you answer from verses 8–9?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We are saved by grace through faith, not by works (verses 8–9). God’s love is a gift, not a wage we collect by being good enough.
dailies.action: Play the gift game once, then read verses 8–10. Each person names one good work they can do this week as a thank-you, not as a payment.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that salvation is your gift, not something we earn. Keep us from boasting, and help us do the good works you prepared for us with glad and grateful hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul says it as clearly as he can: we have been saved by grace, through faith. This is not from ourselves. It is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast. If we could earn our way to God, we would brag about it. Grace shuts that door and opens a better one. Verse 10 does not take the gift back. It shows what the gift is for: we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do. We do not work to get the gift. We work because we have it.
dailies.enochActivity: Game: Can you earn it? A parent holds a small treat. First ask Enoch to “pay” with toys or chores, and shake your head: “That’s not how this gift works.” Then give it freely and say together, “By grace! It’s a gift!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 9, why is salvation “not by works”?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “So that no one can boast” (verse 9).
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 10 says we are created in Christ Jesus to do good works God prepared in advance. How can you do a good work this week as a thank-you, not as a way to get God to accept you?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Pick a real, simple good work — helping at home, telling the truth, being kind to someone left out — and do it because you already belong to Jesus, not to earn his love (verse 10).
dailies.passageText: 8 For it is by grace you have been saved, through faith—and this is not from yourselves, it is the gift of God— 9 not by works, so that no one can boast. 10 For we are God’s handiwork, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance for us to do.

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: God shows his love in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Jesus did not wait until we had cleaned ourselves up.
dailies.verse: But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
dailies.enoch: Say with a parent, “Jesus died for me, even when I was a sinner. That’s how much God loves me!”
dailies.elijah: In Romans 5:6, what were we when Christ died for us?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Powerless,” and he died “for the ungodly” (verse 6).
dailies.jordyn: Why is it good news that Christ died for us “while we were still sinners,” not after we became good enough?
dailies.jordynAnswer: If he had waited until we were good enough, we would still be waiting (verses 6, 8). His love came first, and that is why there is hope for sinners.
dailies.action: Read Romans 5:8 together. Then each person thanks Jesus for dying for them, and if it fits, names one person they can make peace with this week.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for demonstrating your love: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Thank you that we have been reconciled to you through his death. Help us live at peace with you and with one another. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul wants us to see how unusual God’s love is. At just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. Someone might dare to die for a good person, but God did more. He demonstrates his own love in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Because we have been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from God’s wrath through him. We were God’s enemies, and we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son. This is not a small kindness. It is peace with God, paid for by Jesus when we had nothing to offer him.
dailies.enochActivity: Give Enoch a hug “anyway” — not because he just tidied up, but just because he is loved. Say, “God loved us even when we were sinners.”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 8, when did Christ die for us?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “While we were still sinners” (verse 8).
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 10 says we were “God’s enemies” and were “reconciled to him through the death of his Son.” What does “reconciled” mean, and how could you make peace with someone this week the way God has made peace with you?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Reconciled means brought back together, no longer enemies (verse 10). Because God made peace with us through Jesus, we can take a step toward peace with someone we have been at odds with — a sibling, a classmate, or a friend.
dailies.passageText: 6 You see, at just the right time, when we were still powerless, Christ died for the ungodly. 7 Very rarely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person someone might possibly dare to die. 8 But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 9 Since we have now been justified by his blood, how much more shall we be saved from God’s wrath through him! 10 For if, while we were God’s enemies, we were reconciled to him through the death of his Son, how much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved through his life! 11 Not only is this so, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: Jesus took our place. The LORD laid our sin on him, so that in him we could be made right with God.
dailies.verse: God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
dailies.enoch: Point to your heart, then point up, and say, “Jesus took my sin. He paid for me!”
dailies.elijah: In Isaiah 53:5, what was on him that brought us peace?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “The punishment that brought us peace was on him” (verse 5).
dailies.jordyn: 2 Corinthians 5:21 says God made him “who had no sin to be sin for us.” Why does it matter that Jesus had no sin of his own?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He did not pay for his own guilt. He was able to take ours because he had none, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.
dailies.action: Read Isaiah 53:6 and 2 Corinthians 5:21 slowly. Then each person quietly tells the Lord one sin they are glad Jesus paid for, and thanks him.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus had no sin and yet took ours. Thank you that the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and that by his wounds we are healed. Help us trust the one who paid for us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Isaiah spoke of a servant who would carry what was ours. “Surely he took up our pain and bore our suffering.” “He was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed.” We all went astray like sheep, and “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all.” Paul says the same thing in one sentence: God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. Jesus did not pay for his own sin. He had none. He paid for ours. That is what it means that Jesus paid for our sin.
dailies.enochActivity: Use two cups or hands: one “my sin,” one “Jesus.” Move the “sin” hand over to Jesus’ side and say, “He took it for me.” Then smile and say, “By his wounds we are healed.”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In Isaiah 53:6, what have we all done, and what has the LORD laid on him?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way,” and “the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all” (verse 6).
dailies.jordyn2: Someone might say, “My sin is too heavy for God to forgive.” How would you answer from Isaiah 53:6 and 2 Corinthians 5:21?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The LORD has laid on Jesus “the iniquity of us all” (Isaiah 53:6). He took our sin so that in him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21). No one who comes to him is left carrying it alone.
dailies.passageText: 4 Surely he took up our pain and bore our suffering, yet we considered him punished by God, stricken by him, and afflicted. 5 But he was pierced for our transgressions, he was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was on him, and by his wounds we are healed. 6 We all, like sheep, have gone astray, each of us has turned to our own way; and the LORD has laid on him the iniquity of us all. 21 God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: This is love: not that we loved God first, but that he loved us and sent his Son. We can thank him in prayer for that gift.
dailies.verse: This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say, “Thank you, God, for loving me and sending Jesus!”
dailies.elijah: In 1 John 4:10, who loved first — us, or God?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God did. “Not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son” (verse 10).
dailies.jordyn: 1 John 4:10 calls Jesus “an atoning sacrifice for our sins.” In your own words, how does that fit with what we have learned this week about Jesus paying for our sin?
dailies.jordynAnswer: An atoning sacrifice means Jesus gave himself to deal with our sins before God (1 John 4:10). That is how he paid for our sin: he took our place so we could live through him (verse 9).
dailies.action: Read 1 John 4:10 and John 3:16 together. Then go around and let each person pray one short thank-you or one short request.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you loved us first and sent your Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins. Thank you that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. Help us believe you, love you back, and pray for people who do not yet know this gift. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: John tells us what love looks like. “This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him.” “This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.” We did not start this. God did. Jesus used the same words: “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.” God did not send his Son to condemn the world, but to save the world through him. Prayer today is simple: we tell God thank you for a love that came first, and we ask for help to believe and to love him back.
dailies.enochActivity: Pray with Enoch one sentence at a time: “Thank you, God, for loving me. Thank you for sending Jesus. Help me love you back. Amen.”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In John 3:16, what happens for whoever believes in God’s Son?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They “shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).
dailies.jordyn2: John 3:17 says God did not send his Son to condemn the world, but to save it. How can that shape the way you pray tonight for someone who does not yet trust Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We can pray for them the way God came to the world: not first to condemn, but that they would be saved through Jesus (John 3:16–17). Ask God to help them believe.
dailies.passageText: 9 This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him. 10 This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins. 16 For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him.

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: We were dead in our sins, but God is rich in mercy. Jesus paid for our sin, and salvation is a gift of grace through faith, not something we earn.
dailies.verse: For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
dailies.enoch: Ask, “Who paid for my sin?” (Jesus!) “Is it a gift or something I earn?” (A gift!)
dailies.elijah: In John 3:16, what did God give, and what do we do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: God “gave his one and only Son,” and “whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16).
dailies.jordyn: This week we read Ephesians 2, Romans 5, Isaiah 53, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and 1 John 4. In one or two sentences, what is grace?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Grace is God’s gift: we were dead in our sins, and Jesus paid for them, so we are saved through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 5:8).
dailies.action: Read John 3:16 together, then each person shares one thing they learned this week and one way they want to thank God for his gift.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for loving the world and giving your Son. Thank you that Jesus paid for our sin, and that whoever believes in him has eternal life. Help us trust this gift and live as people who have already been made alive with Christ. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week. We were dead in our transgressions and sins, but God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ. It is by grace we have been saved, through faith — the gift of God, not by works. While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. The LORD laid on him the iniquity of us all. God made him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son. John 3:16 gathers it up: God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life.
dailies.enochActivity: Review the gift game or the cross-and-heart picture from earlier in the week. Point and say, “Jesus paid. God loves me. It’s a gift!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 17, why did God send his Son into the world?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Not… to condemn the world, but to save the world through him” (verse 17).
dailies.jordyn2: If salvation is a gift, what is one way you will live this coming week as someone who has already been loved and paid for, not as someone trying to earn God’s yes?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: tell the truth, forgive, serve, pray, or stop boasting in yourself. The point is to live from the gift (Ephesians 2:10; John 3:16), not to buy it.
dailies.passageText: 16 For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life. 17 For God did not send his Son into the world to condemn the world, but to save the world through him.

weeks.title: Faith and repentance (the lost son)
weeks.selectLabel: Week 14 · Faith and repentance (the lost son)
weeks.nextUp: Week 15 · Prayer: talking with our Father
weeks.bigIdea: Jesus tells about a son who wasted what his father gave him, came to his senses, and said, “I have sinned.” The father ran to welcome him home. That is a picture of repentance and faith: we turn from our sin and trust the Father who comes to meet us.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 14 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Luke 15:11–32 out loud in two parts, then read Mark 1:15, where Jesus says, “Repent and believe the good news!”

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 11 Jesus continued: “There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them. 13 “Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs. 16 He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. 17 “When he came to his senses, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! 18 I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’ 20 So he got up and went to his father. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 “But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ So they began to celebrate.

25 “Meanwhile, the older son was in the field. When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing. 26 So he called one of the servants and asked him what was going on. 27 ‘Your brother has come,’ he replied, ‘and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has him back safe and sound.’ 28 “The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. 29 But he answered his father, ‘Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. 30 But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!’ 31 “‘My son,’ the father said, ‘you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. 32 But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’”
15 “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!”

story: Last week we learned that we were dead in our sins, and that Jesus paid for our sin. Salvation is a gift of grace we cannot earn. This week we ask: how do we come home to God? Jesus tells a story about a father and two sons to help us see.

The younger son asked for his share of the family’s goods while his father was still living, then went far away and wasted it all. When he had nothing left, he was so hungry he wanted to eat the pods he was feeding to pigs. Then he came to his senses. He said, “I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.” That is repentance: he turned around, told the truth about his sin, and went home.

While he was still a long way off, his father saw him, ran to him, threw his arms around him, and kissed him. The son started his confession, but the father was already calling for the best robe, a ring, and a feast. “This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” The father did not make him earn his way back. He welcomed him with joy.

The older son had stayed home and worked, and he became angry. He would not go in to the party. The father went out to him too, and said, “You are always with me, and everything I have is yours. But we had to celebrate, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again.” Coming home is a gift. Being “the good one” can keep a person standing outside the feast.

Jesus also said, “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!” Faith and repentance belong together: we turn from going our own way, and we trust the Father who runs to meet us because of Jesus.
weeks.enochLine: I can tell God I’m sorry and come home. My Father runs to me!
enochActivities: Activity: The long way home. Have Enoch take a few steps away, then turn around and run back into a parent’s hug. Say together, “I’m sorry. I’m home! The Father runs to me!”
Activity: The welcome feast. Set a napkin or paper “robe” on Enoch’s shoulders and say, “You were lost, and now you’re found. Let’s celebrate!”
elijahQuestions: In Luke 15:18, what did the younger son decide to say to his father?
In Luke 15:20, what did the father do when he saw his son still a long way off?
In Luke 15:24, how did the father describe what had happened to his son?
In Mark 1:15, what two things did Jesus say to do because the kingdom of God has come near?
jordynQuestions: The son planned a speech about being a hired servant (Luke 15:18–21). What does the father’s welcome in verses 20–24 tell you about how God receives people who repent?
The older son was angry and would not go in (Luke 15:28–30). What was wrong with the way he thought about his father and his brother?
Jesus said, “Repent and believe the good news” (Mark 1:15). How do both parts matter if someone only says “sorry” but does not trust the Father, or only says they believe but will not turn?
weeks.jordynApplication: Repentance is telling the truth and turning toward the Father; faith is trusting his welcome (Luke 15:18–24; Mark 1:15). This week, if you need to confess something, do not delay and do not try to earn your way back. Tell God, and if you have wronged someone at home, go to them too. Then thank the Father that he runs to meet you.
elijahAnswers: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you” (Luke 15:18). He also planned to say he was no longer worthy to be called a son.
“He ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him” (Luke 15:20).
“This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found” (Luke 15:24).
“Repent and believe the good news!” (Mark 1:15).
jordynAnswers: The father ran, embraced him, and restored him as a son with a robe, a ring, and a feast before the speech was even finished (Luke 15:20–24). God welcomes repenting people with joy, not as hired hands who must earn their way back.
He treated his years at home like unpaid labor, and he would not share his father’s joy that a lost brother was found (Luke 15:28–32). He was close to the house and far from the father’s heart.

Repentance is turning; faith is trusting the good news (Mark 1:15). Sorry without trust is only words; belief that will not turn is not the coming-home Jesus describes. We need both: turn from our own way and trust the Father who runs to meet us.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she had a chance to confess something and to thank God for his welcome. If it is fitting, share one place you needed to come home to the Father too, and pray for each other.
weeks.prayer: Dear Father, thank you for running to meet us when we have sinned and come home. Thank you that Jesus said, “Repent and believe the good news.” We confess that we have gone our own way. Please forgive us, welcome us, and give us joy like the father’s joy when the lost son was found. Help us not to stand outside like the older brother. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: The lost son came to his senses, said “I have sinned,” and started home. While he was still a long way off, his father ran to him.
dailies.verse: But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.
dailies.enoch: Take a few steps away, then run back for a hug and say, “I’m sorry! I’m home!”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 15:17, what happened to the younger son in the far country?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “He came to his senses” (verse 17).
dailies.jordyn: The father ran while the son was “still a long way off” (verse 20). What does that tell you about God’s welcome when someone begins to turn back?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God’s compassion meets us before we have finished getting home or making a perfect speech (verses 20–24). He is not waiting at the door with his arms crossed.
dailies.action: Read Luke 15:20–24 together. Then each person thanks the Father for one way he has welcomed your family.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you are filled with compassion and that you run to meet us when we come home. We have sinned against heaven and against you. Welcome us, and make our house a place of that same joy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we heard Jesus’ story of a father and two sons. The younger son asked for his share, went far away, and wasted everything. When he was hungry and alone, “he came to his senses.” He did not make excuses. He planned to say, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.” That is repentance: turning around and telling the truth. And here is the surprise of grace: “While he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son.” The son started his speech, but the father was already calling for the best robe, a ring, and a feast. “This son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.” Coming home is not earning a hired place. It is being welcomed as a child.
dailies.enochActivity: Practice the welcome: a parent pretends to see Enoch “a long way off,” then runs to hug him. Say, “The Father runs to me!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 21, what did the son say to his father?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son” (verse 21).
dailies.jordyn2: The father said the son “was dead and is alive again” (verse 24). How does that fit with what we learned last week about being made alive with Christ?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Last week we heard that we were dead in our sins and God made us alive with Christ. This story pictures the same gift: a lost, as-good-as-dead son is alive again because the father welcomes him home.
dailies.passageText: 11 Jesus continued: “There was a man who had two sons. 12 The younger one said to his father, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them. 13 “Not long after that, the younger son got together all he had, set off for a distant country and there squandered his wealth in wild living. 14 After he had spent everything, there was a severe famine in that whole country, and he began to be in need. 15 So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him to his fields to feed pigs. 16 He longed to fill his stomach with the pods that the pigs were eating, but no one gave him anything. 17 “When he came to his senses, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! 18 I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’ 20 So he got up and went to his father. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 “But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ So they began to celebrate.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: Repentance is turning around. The son did not stay in the far country making promises. He got up and went home.
dailies.verse: I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
dailies.enoch: Turn around in a circle, then walk toward a parent and say, “I will go back to my Father!”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 15:18, what did the son say he would do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “I will set out and go back to my father and say… Father, I have sinned” (verse 18).
dailies.jordyn: What is the difference between only feeling sorry and doing what the son does in verses 18–20?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Feeling sorry can stay in the far country. The son got up, went, and confessed, “I have sinned.” Repentance includes turning and coming home.
dailies.action: Play the far-country game once, then read verses 18–20. If anyone in the family has something to make right, help them take a first step today.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that repentance means we can get up and come home. Give us courage to tell the truth and to turn, and thank you that you run to meet us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The son came to his senses in a hard place, among the pigs. He remembered his father’s house, and he made a decision: “I will set out and go back to my father.” Repentance is not only feeling sad. It is turning around and going home, telling the truth: “I have sinned.” Jesus wants us to see both the son’s turn and the father’s run. If we only feel bad and never turn, we are still in the far country. If we think we have to finish a perfect speech before God will love us, we have not yet seen the father run.
dailies.enochActivity: Game: Far country, home. Mark two spots on the floor. Stand in the “far country,” then on the count of three everyone turns and runs “home” for a hug. Laugh, then say, “Repent means turn around and come home!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 20, did the son actually go, or only talk about going?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “So he got up and went to his father” (verse 20). He really went.
dailies.jordyn2: Is there something this week you need to “get up and go” about — a confession to God, or to someone at home — instead of only meaning to?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary. The point is to take a real step like verse 20, not to stay in the far country with a plan you never start.
dailies.passageText: 17 “When he came to his senses, he said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have food to spare, and here I am starving to death! 18 I will set out and go back to my father and say to him: Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. 19 I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.’ 20 So he got up and went to his father. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 “But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ So they began to celebrate.

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: The older son stayed close to the house and far from the father’s joy. The father went out to him too, and invited him into the feast.
dailies.verse: But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.
dailies.enoch: When someone is happy, can you be happy too? Practice a cheer: “Let’s celebrate! He was lost, and now he’s found!”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 15:28, what did the older son refuse to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “He refused to go in” (verse 28). He was angry.
dailies.jordyn: The older son said “this son of yours” (verse 30) instead of “my brother.” Why does that matter?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He would not claim his brother. He wanted the father to take his side against the one who had come home. The father answers, “this brother of yours” (verse 32).
dailies.action: Read Luke 15:31–32 together. Then each person names one person they can rejoice over, or one place they have been standing outside the feast.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you come out to the angry older son as well as to the lost younger one. Keep us from refusing to go in. Give us your joy when the lost are found. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The older son was in the field when the music started. He heard about the feast for his brother and became angry. He would not go in. Notice that the father went out to him too. The older son listed his years of work and complained that he had never even received a young goat. He would not call the younger one “my brother,” only “this son of yours.” The father said, “My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours.” “But we had to celebrate… because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again.” You can stay near the house and still miss the father’s heart. Faith is not only avoiding the far country. It is sharing the Father’s joy when a lost person comes home.
dailies.enochActivity: Make a tiny “feast” with a snack. Invite everyone to sit down. If someone hangs back, a parent goes to them like the father and says, “Come in! Everything I have is yours.”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 31, what did the father tell the older son?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “My son, you are always with me, and everything I have is yours” (verse 31).
dailies.jordyn2: When have you been more like the older son than the younger one — sure you have done the right things, and slow to rejoice when God is kind to someone else?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary. The warning is that working hard and staying home is not the same as sharing the father’s heart (verses 28–32).
dailies.passageText: 25 “Meanwhile, the older son was in the field. When he came near the house, he heard music and dancing. 26 So he called one of the servants and asked him what was going on. 27 ‘Your brother has come,’ he replied, ‘and your father has killed the fattened calf because he has him back safe and sound.’ 28 “The older brother became angry and refused to go in. So his father went out and pleaded with him. 29 But he answered his father, ‘Look! All these years I’ve been slaving for you and never disobeyed your orders. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends. 30 But when this son of yours who has squandered your property with prostitutes comes home, you kill the fattened calf for him!’ 31 “‘My son,’ the father said, ‘you are always with me, and everything I have is yours. 32 But we had to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’”

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: Jesus says the kingdom of God has come near. The right response is two words that belong together: repent, and believe the good news.
dailies.verse: “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!”
dailies.enoch: Hold up one finger and say, “Repent — turn!” Hold up a second finger and say, “Believe the good news!”
dailies.elijah: In Mark 1:15, what has come near?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “The kingdom of God” (Mark 1:15).
dailies.jordyn: Why does Jesus put “repent” and “believe” together, instead of only one or the other?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Turning without trust is just trying harder. Believing without turning leaves us in the far country. Jesus calls us to both (Mark 1:15), like the son who came home and trusted the father’s welcome.
dailies.action: Read Mark 1:15 twice. Then each person names one way they need to turn, and one part of the good news they will trust today.
dailies.prayer: Lord Jesus, you said the kingdom of God has come near. Help us repent and believe the good news. Turn us from our own way, wipe out our sins, and send times of refreshing from the Lord. Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus did not only tell a story about coming home. He also gave a clear call: “The time has come. The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!” Repent means turn. Believe means trust the good news — the news we heard last week, that Jesus paid for our sin, and the news in the story, that the Father runs to welcome us. Peter later said, “Repent, then, and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped out, that times of refreshing may come from the Lord.” Turning and trusting are not two different religions. They are how we come home.
dailies.enochActivity: Two-step challenge: take one step to the side (“I was going my own way”), then turn and take a step toward a parent (“I trust you”). Say Mark 1:15 together: “Repent and believe the good news!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In Acts 3:19, what happens when we repent and turn to God?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Our “sins may be wiped out,” and “times of refreshing may come from the Lord” (Acts 3:19).
dailies.jordyn2: Acts 3:19 says sins can be “wiped out.” If you have already trusted Jesus, how can this still be a daily call — and if you are still coming, what is a first step?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Followers of Jesus still turn when we sin, and we keep trusting the same good news. If you are still coming, the first step is the son’s step: tell the truth and come to the Father. Parents can help you pray.
dailies.passageText: 15 “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!” 19 Repent, then, and turn to God, so that your sins may be wiped out, that times of refreshing may come from the Lord,

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: A repenting heart asks God for mercy. We can pray David’s words: have mercy, create a pure heart, and receive a broken and contrite heart.
dailies.verse: My sacrifice, O God, is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart you, God, will not despise.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and pray, “Have mercy on me, O God. Give me a clean heart.”
dailies.elijah: In Psalm 51:1, what does David ask for, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love” (verse 1). He asks for mercy because of God’s love, not because he has earned it.
dailies.jordyn: David says, “Against you, you only, have I sinned” (verse 4). What does he mean, if our sin also hurts other people?
dailies.jordynAnswer: All sin is first against God, even when it also wounds people (verse 4). We confess to God, and we still need to make things right with those we have hurt, like the son who said he had sinned “against heaven and against you.”
dailies.action: Read Psalm 51:1 and 51:10 together, then let each person pray one short sentence of confession or one sentence of thanks for mercy.
dailies.prayer: Have mercy on us, O God, according to your unfailing love. Wash us clean, create in us a pure heart, and do not despise our broken and contrite hearts. Thank you that you run to meet us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: David prayed this after he had sinned badly and then told the truth about it. He did not ask God to pay him what he had earned. He asked for mercy: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love.” He asked to be washed clean. He said, “Against you, you only, have I sinned.” He asked for a new start inside: “Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” And he told God what the Lord will not despise: “a broken and contrite heart.” That is the younger son’s heart, and it is a good prayer for a family that wants to come home.
dailies.enochActivity: Pray Psalm 51:10 with Enoch, one short phrase at a time: “Create in me a pure heart, O God.” Then a hug, because God does not despise a sorry heart.
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 10, what does David ask God to create?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “A pure heart,” and he asks God to “renew a steadfast spirit within me” (verse 10).
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 17 says God will not despise a broken and contrite heart. How can that make it safer to pray honestly tonight, instead of hiding?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God does not push away a truly sorry heart (verse 17). We can tell him the truth, like the lost son, and ask him to create a pure heart in us.
dailies.passageText: 1 Have mercy on me, O God, according to your unfailing love; according to your great compassion blot out my transgressions. 2 Wash away all my iniquity and cleanse me from my sin. 3 For I know my transgressions, and my sin is always before me. 4 Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight; so you are right in your verdict and justified when you judge. 10 Create in me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me. 17 My sacrifice, O God, is a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart you, God, will not despise.

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: The lost son came home, and the father ran to meet him. Jesus says, “Repent and believe the good news.” We turn from our sin and trust the Father who welcomes us.
dailies.verse: But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him.
dailies.enoch: Ask, “What did the father do when he saw his son?” (He ran!) “What does Jesus tell us to do?” (Repent and believe!)
dailies.elijah: In Luke 15:20, when did the father run to his son?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “While he was still a long way off” (verse 20).
dailies.jordyn: This week we also met the older brother. Why does a recap of the lost son need that part of the story too?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can stay near the house and still refuse the father’s joy (Luke 15:28–32). Coming home is for the runaway and for the one who is angry that grace is being given away.
dailies.action: Read Luke 15:20 and Mark 1:15 together. Then each person shares one thing they learned this week and one way they want to come home to the Father.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for running to meet us while we were still a long way off. Help us repent and believe the good news, and make our family quick to come home and quick to celebrate. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week. The younger son came to his senses, said “I have sinned,” and went home. The father ran, embraced him, and said he was dead and is alive again, lost and is found. The older son would not go in, and the father went out to him too. Jesus calls us to the same coming-home: “Repent and believe the good news.” David taught us to pray for mercy and a pure heart. This is how we come to the Father after last week’s news that Jesus paid for our sin: we turn, we trust, and we are welcomed.
dailies.enochActivity: Replay the welcome hug or the far-country game one last time. Say together, “I was lost, and I am found. The Father runs to me!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In Mark 1:15, what two things does Jesus tell us to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Repent and believe the good news!” (Mark 1:15).
dailies.jordyn2: How will you practice both repenting and believing this coming week — at home, at school, or when you fail?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: confess quickly, trust the Father’s welcome instead of hiding, rejoice when someone else is forgiven, pray Psalm 51. The call is still Mark 1:15.
dailies.passageText: 20 So he got up and went to his father. “But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and was filled with compassion for him; he ran to his son, threw his arms around him and kissed him. 21 “The son said to him, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’ 22 “But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet. 23 Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let’s have a feast and celebrate. 24 For this son of mine was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’ So they began to celebrate. 15 “The time has come,” he said. “The kingdom of God has come near. Repent and believe the good news!”

weeks.title: Prayer: talking with our Father
weeks.selectLabel: Week 15 · Prayer: talking with our Father
weeks.nextUp: Week 16 · The Bible is God's Word
weeks.bigIdea: Jesus teaches us how to talk with our Father. We pray to our Father in heaven, not to be seen. We ask, seek, and knock, because our Father gives good gifts. We come humbly, like the tax collector who said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.”
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 15 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Matthew 6:5–15 out loud, then Luke 11:9–13, then Luke 18:9–14, the story of two men who went to pray.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 5 “And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full. 6 But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. 7 And when you pray, do not keep on babbling like pagans, for they think they will be heard because of their many words. 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. 9 “This, then, is how you should pray: “‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, 10 your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us today our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ 14 For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. 15 But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins.

9 “So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened. 11 “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? 12 Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? 13 If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

9 To some who were confident of their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else, Jesus told this parable: 10 “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. 11 The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. 12 I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.’ 13 “But the tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’ 14 “I tell you that this man, rather than the other, went home justified before God. For all those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.”

story: Last week we learned that we come home to God by repenting and believing. The lost son said, “I have sinned,” and his father ran to meet him. This week we ask: how do we talk with that same Father? Jesus teaches his disciples how to pray.

Jesus said, “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites,” who love to stand and pray so people will see them. And do not keep piling up empty words, as if God will listen only if we talk long enough. “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Then Jesus gave us a prayer that begins, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.” We ask for his kingdom, our daily bread, forgiveness, and help when we are tempted.

Jesus also said, “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.” If even earthly fathers know how to give good gifts to their children, “how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” We can come to God as children who are not afraid to knock.

Jesus told about two men who went up to the temple to pray. One was proud of himself and looked down on the other. The tax collector stood far off, would not even look up, and said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” Jesus said that man went home justified before God. “Those who humble themselves will be exalted.” Talking with our Father is not bragging. It is asking for mercy.

So this is how we talk with God. We come to our Father in heaven. We do not put on a show. We ask, seek, and knock. We tell the truth and ask for mercy. And we learn to bring our worries to him with thanksgiving, and to rejoice, pray, and give thanks in all kinds of days.
weeks.enochLine: I can talk with my Father. He loves to hear me!
enochActivities: Activity: Our Father. Fold hands and say together, “Our Father in heaven, you are holy. I can talk with you!”
Activity: Ask, seek, knock. Let Enoch knock on a door. When it opens, say, “Our Father gives good gifts!”
elijahQuestions: In Matthew 6:9, how did Jesus say we should begin our prayer?
In Matthew 6:5, why do the hypocrites love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners?
In Luke 11:9, what three things did Jesus tell us to do?
In Luke 18:13, what did the tax collector pray?
jordynQuestions: Jesus said not to keep on babbling like pagans, because “your Father knows what you need before you ask him” (Matthew 6:7–8). If he already knows, why does he still teach us to pray the words in verses 9–13?
In Luke 11:11–13, Jesus compares earthly fathers with “your Father in heaven.” What good gift does he say the Father will give, and what does that teach you about asking?
The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like the tax collector (Luke 18:11–14). Which man went home justified, and why?
weeks.jordynApplication: Prayer is talking with our Father: not a show, not empty words, and not bragging. This week, practice the prayer Jesus taught, and also practice a humble “have mercy on me” prayer. When you are worried, present your request to God with thanksgiving (Matthew 6:9–13; Luke 18:13; Philippians 4:6–7).
elijahAnswers: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9).
“To be seen by others” (Matthew 6:5).
Ask, seek, and knock (Luke 11:9).
“God, have mercy on me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13).
jordynAnswers: Prayer is not informing God of news he missed. Jesus gives us words to talk with our Father, honor his name, ask for his kingdom and daily bread, and confess our sins (Matthew 6:8–13). He wants us to come to him.
The Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13). If even flawed fathers give good gifts, we can ask our Father with confidence.

The tax collector went home justified, not the Pharisee. “All those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted” (Luke 18:14). He asked for mercy instead of trusting his own righteousness.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she practiced talking with the Father — the Lord’s Prayer, a “have mercy on me” prayer, or a worried request with thanksgiving. If it is fitting, share one way you talked with the Father too, and pray together.
weeks.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Thank you that we can talk with you, and that you know what we need before we ask. Teach us to ask, seek, and knock. Have mercy on us, sinners, and give us your Holy Spirit. Help us bring our worries to you with thanksgiving. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: Jesus teaches us how to talk with our Father. We do not pray to be seen. We pray, “Our Father in heaven.”
dailies.verse: “This, then, is how you should pray: “‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say, “Our Father in heaven, you are holy. I can talk with you!”
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 6:5, why do the hypocrites love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “To be seen by others” (verse 5).
dailies.jordyn: Jesus says your Father “knows what you need before you ask him” (verse 8). If he already knows, why does Jesus still teach us to pray the words in verses 9–13?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Prayer is not informing God of news he missed. It is talking with our Father, honoring his name, asking for his kingdom and daily bread, and confessing our sins (verses 8–13). He wants us to come to him, not to perform for people.
dailies.action: Read Matthew 6:9–13 together slowly. Then let each person pray one short line from the prayer in their own words.
dailies.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us today our daily bread, and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we heard Jesus teach his disciples how to pray. He said, “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites,” who love to pray in public “to be seen by others.” And do not “keep on babbling like pagans,” as if many words could make God listen. “Your Father knows what you need before you ask him.” Then Jesus gave us words to use: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.” We talk with a Father. We ask for his kingdom, our daily bread, forgiveness, and help against temptation. Prayer is not a show. It is a child talking with a Father who already knows and still wants to hear us.
dailies.enochActivity: Practice the opening: a parent starts, “Our Father in heaven,” and Enoch says, “You are holy!” Then a hug, because we get to talk with our Father.
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 9, how did Jesus say we should begin our prayer?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (verse 9).
dailies.jordyn2: In verses 14–15 Jesus talks about forgiving others after teaching us to pray. How does that fit with “forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors” (verse 12)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The prayer we say with our mouths should match the way we treat people. Jesus says if we forgive others, our Father will forgive us, and if we refuse to forgive, we should not expect to receive that same mercy (verses 12, 14–15).
dailies.passageText: 5 “And when you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the street corners to be seen by others. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward in full. 6 But when you pray, go into your room, close the door and pray to your Father, who is unseen. Then your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you. 7 And when you pray, do not keep on babbling like pagans, for they think they will be heard because of their many words. 8 Do not be like them, for your Father knows what you need before you ask him. 9 “This, then, is how you should pray: “‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, 10 your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us today our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ 14 For if you forgive other people when they sin against you, your heavenly Father will also forgive you. 15 But if you do not forgive others their sins, your Father will not forgive your sins.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: Jesus says, “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.” Our Father gives good gifts.
dailies.verse: “So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.
dailies.enoch: Knock on a door three times and say, “Ask! Seek! Knock! My Father hears me!”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 11:9, what three things does Jesus tell us to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Ask, seek, and knock (verse 9).
dailies.jordyn: Jesus asks whether a father would give a snake instead of a fish, or a scorpion instead of an egg (verses 11–12). What is he teaching about God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Even earthly fathers, who are “evil,” know how to give good gifts. “How much more” will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (verses 11–13). We can ask with confidence, because our Father is better than the best dad we know.
dailies.action: Play the ask-seek-knock game once, then read Luke 11:9–13. Each person asks the Father for one good gift, and thanks him that he loves to give.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you tell us to ask, seek, and knock, and that you give good gifts. Thank you that you give the Holy Spirit to those who ask you. Help us come to you with confidence. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus had been praying, and his disciples asked him to teach them to pray. After he gave them words to use, he told them to keep coming: “Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you.” Everyone who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened. Then he pictured a child asking a father for a fish or an egg. A good father does not answer that request with a snake or a scorpion. “If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” We do not have to be afraid to ask. Our Father is generous.
dailies.enochActivity: Game: Ask, seek, knock. Hide a small treat or toy. Let Enoch ask, “May I have it?” then seek (look), then knock on a door. When it opens, say, “Our Father gives good gifts!”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 13, what good gift does Jesus say the Father in heaven will give to those who ask him?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “The Holy Spirit” (verse 13).
dailies.jordyn2: Jesus says “everyone who asks receives” (verse 10). How do you hold that together with times it feels as if a door has not opened yet?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Jesus is teaching us to keep asking a good Father, not to treat God like a vending machine. The best gift he names here is the Holy Spirit (verses 9–13). We keep knocking because we trust the Father’s character, even while we wait for particular answers.
dailies.passageText: 9 “So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. 10 For everyone who asks receives; the one who seeks finds; and to the one who knocks, the door will be opened. 11 “Which of you fathers, if your son asks for a fish, will give him a snake instead? 12 Or if he asks for an egg, will give him a scorpion? 13 If you then, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father in heaven give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!”

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: Two men went to the temple to pray. The tax collector would not even look up to heaven. He said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner,” and he went home justified.
dailies.verse: But the tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’
dailies.enoch: Put a hand on your heart and pray, “God, have mercy on me. I need you.”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 18:13, what did the tax collector say in his prayer?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “God, have mercy on me, a sinner” (verse 13).
dailies.jordyn: The Pharisee thanked God that he was not like other people, and he listed his fasting and tithing (verses 11–12). Why did he not go home justified, according to verse 14?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus said, “All those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted” (verse 14). The Pharisee trusted his own righteousness and looked down on others (verse 9). The tax collector asked for mercy.
dailies.action: Read Luke 18:9–14 together. Then each person prays a short “have mercy on me” prayer, and thanks God that he hears a humble heart.
dailies.prayer: God, have mercy on us, sinners. We do not come to you proud of ourselves. Thank you that those who humble themselves will be exalted, and that you hear a prayer for mercy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Last week we heard a lost son come home and say, “I have sinned.” Today Jesus tells about two men who went up to the temple to pray. One was a Pharisee who was confident of his own righteousness and looked down on others. He thanked God that he was not like the tax collector, and he named his fasting and his gifts. The tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven. He beat his breast and said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner.” Jesus said this man, not the other, went home justified before God. “For all those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.” Talking with our Father is not bragging. It is asking for mercy.
dailies.enochActivity: Two postures: stand tall and fold your arms (the proud prayer), then bow your head, hand on your heart, and say, “God, have mercy on me.” Talk about which prayer Jesus said God welcomed.
dailies.elijah2: In verse 14, which man went home justified before God?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The tax collector, not the Pharisee (verse 14).
dailies.jordyn2: How does this story fit with last week’s lost son, who said, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you”?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Both men tell the truth about their need and come asking for mercy, not payment. The Father runs to the lost son, and God justifies the tax collector who says, “Have mercy on me, a sinner.” Proud people who trust their own record stay outside that welcome (Luke 18:9–14).
dailies.passageText: 9 To some who were confident of their own righteousness and looked down on everyone else, Jesus told this parable: 10 “Two men went up to the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. 11 The Pharisee stood by himself and prayed: ‘God, I thank you that I am not like other people—robbers, evildoers, adulterers—or even like this tax collector. 12 I fast twice a week and give a tenth of all I get.’ 13 “But the tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’ 14 “I tell you that this man, rather than the other, went home justified before God. For all those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.”

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: When we are anxious, Jesus’ people do not have to hold it all inside. We can tell our Father, with thanksgiving, and he gives peace.
dailies.verse: Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.
dailies.enoch: When you feel worried, put your hands out as if you are giving the worry to God and say, “Father, I give this to you. Thank you.”
dailies.elijah: In Philippians 4:6, what should we do instead of being anxious about anything?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “In every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God” (verse 6).
dailies.jordyn: Verse 6 says we present our requests “with thanksgiving.” Why does thanksgiving belong in a worried prayer?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thanksgiving remembers that we are talking with a Father who already cares for us, not only listing problems. We ask, and we also thank him. Then “the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (verses 6–7).
dailies.action: Read Philippians 4:6–7 twice. Then each person names one worry to give the Father and one thing to thank him for.
dailies.prayer: Father, we do not want to be anxious about anything. In every situation we present our requests to you, with thanksgiving. Please guard our hearts and minds with your peace in Christ Jesus. Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus taught us to ask our Father for daily bread and for help. Paul teaches the same kind of talking with God when we feel anxious. “Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God.” We do not pretend we have no worries. We bring them to our Father, and we thank him as we ask. The promise is not that every hard thing disappears today. The promise is this: “And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.” Today’s challenge is simple: when a worry rises, stop and pray, and thank God for one gift in the same breath.
dailies.enochActivity: Worry-handoff: hold a small stone or coin as a “worry,” then place it in a parent’s hands and say, “Father, I give this to you. Thank you.” The parent says, “He hears you.”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 7, what will the peace of God guard?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (verse 7).
dailies.jordyn2: How does this fit with Jesus teaching us to ask our Father for daily bread (Matthew 6:11) and not to keep babbling as if God were hard of hearing?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Both passages invite honest, thankful asking, not a performance. We present requests because our Father cares, and we add thanksgiving because he already knows and already gives good gifts. His peace, not our many words, guards us (Philippians 4:6–7; Matthew 6:7–11).
dailies.passageText: 6 Do not be anxious about anything, but in every situation, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. 7 And the peace of God, which transcends all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: Talking with our Father is not only for hard days. God’s people learn a simple way of life: rejoice, pray, and give thanks.
dailies.verse: Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Clap once and say, “Rejoice!” Fold your hands and say, “Pray!” Open your hands and say, “Thank you, Father!”
dailies.elijah: In 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18, what three things does God tell us to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances” (verses 16–18).
dailies.jordyn: Verse 18 says to give thanks “in all circumstances,” and that this is “God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.” Does that mean we must feel happy about every hard thing?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It means we can still talk with our Father and thank him in every kind of day, not only easy ones (verses 16–18). Thanksgiving in hard circumstances is trust, not pretend. We rejoice, we pray, and we give thanks because we belong to Christ Jesus.
dailies.action: Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18 together. Then go around three times: one rejoice, one short prayer, and one thank-you.
