dailies.prayer: Father, teach us to rejoice always, to pray continually, and to give thanks in all circumstances. This is your will for us in Christ Jesus. Make our home a place of that kind of talking with you. Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul gives the family of Jesus a short pattern for everyday life with the Father: “Rejoice always, pray continually, give thanks in all circumstances.” These are three short sentences, but they describe a whole way of living. We do not wait for a perfect day before we rejoice. We do not save prayer for emergencies. We do not wait until everything is fixed before we say thank you. “For this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.” Today we practice that pattern out loud, so it can become the habit of our house.
dailies.enochActivity: Three motions: clap (“Rejoice always”), fold hands (“Pray continually”), open hands (“Give thanks”). Repeat once, then pray, “Thank you, Father, for today.”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 18, why are we told to give thanks in all circumstances?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “For this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (verse 18).
dailies.jordyn2: How do “pray continually” and Jesus’ warning not to “keep on babbling like pagans” (Matthew 6:7) fit together?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Continual prayer is a life of talking with the Father, not a pile of empty phrases meant to get God’s attention. Jesus already said our Father knows what we need. So we keep coming, simply and often, with joy and thanks (Matthew 6:7–8; 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18).
dailies.passageText: 16 Rejoice always, 17 pray continually, 18 give thanks in all circumstances; for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus.

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: We talk with our Father. Jesus taught us to pray “Our Father in heaven,” to ask, seek, and knock, and to come humbly, like the tax collector who asked for mercy.
dailies.verse: “This, then, is how you should pray: “‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name,
dailies.enoch: Ask, “Who do we talk to when we pray?” (Our Father!) “What did the tax collector ask for?” (Mercy!)
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 6:9, how does Jesus tell us to begin our prayer?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name” (verse 9).
dailies.jordyn: This week we also heard the tax collector’s prayer and the call to ask, seek, and knock. Why does a recap of “talking with our Father” need both the humble prayer and the confident asking?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We come as sinners who need mercy (Luke 18:13–14), and we come as children who may ask a generous Father (Luke 11:9–13). Humility and confidence belong together when we pray to our Father in heaven.
dailies.action: Read Matthew 6:9–13 together. Then each person shares one thing they learned this week and one way they want to talk with the Father this coming week.
dailies.prayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. Thank you that we may ask, seek, and knock, and that you give good gifts. Have mercy on us, and teach us to pray with thanks and peace. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week. Jesus taught us not to pray to be seen, and not to pile up empty words. He gave us a prayer that begins, “Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.” He told us to ask, seek, and knock, because our Father gives good gifts, even the Holy Spirit, to those who ask him. He told a story of a tax collector who would not even look up, but said, “God, have mercy on me, a sinner,” and went home justified. Paul taught us to bring our worries to God with thanksgiving, and to rejoice, pray, and give thanks in all circumstances. Talking with our Father is a gift. We come humbly, and we come as loved children.
dailies.enochActivity: Recap motions: fold hands (“Our Father”), knock on a door (“Ask, seek, knock”), hand on heart (“Have mercy on me”). Then a family hug and, “We can talk with our Father!”
dailies.elijah2: In Luke 18:13, what did the tax collector ask God for?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “God, have mercy on me, a sinner” (Luke 18:13).
dailies.jordyn2: Philippians 4:6–7 says to present requests “with thanksgiving,” and 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says to give thanks “in all circumstances.” How does thanksgiving change the way a family talks with the Father?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Thanksgiving keeps prayer from becoming only a list of wants or worries. We still ask for mercy and for daily bread, and we also remember the Father’s gifts and his will for us in Christ Jesus (Philippians 4:6–7; 1 Thessalonians 5:16–18).
dailies.passageText: 9 “This, then, is how you should pray: “‘Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name, 10 your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. 11 Give us today our daily bread. 12 And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. 13 And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.’ “So I say to you: Ask and it will be given to you; seek and you will find; knock and the door will be opened to you. “But the tax collector stood at a distance. He would not even look up to heaven, but beat his breast and said, ‘God, have mercy on me, a sinner.’

weeks.title: The Bible is God's Word
weeks.selectLabel: Week 16 · The Bible is God's Word
weeks.nextUp: Week 17 · God's design for marriage and family
weeks.bigIdea: The Bible is God’s Word. All Scripture is God-breathed, able to make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. God’s Word is a lamp for our feet, and we live on every word that comes from the mouth of God.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 16 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read 2 Timothy 3:14–17 out loud, then Psalm 119:97–105, then Matthew 4:1–4, where Jesus answers the tempter with God’s Word.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

97 Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long. 98 Your commands are always with me and make me wiser than my enemies. 99 I have more insight than all my teachers, for I meditate on your statutes. 100 I have more understanding than the elders, for I obey your precepts. 101 I have kept my feet from every evil path so that I might obey your word. 102 I have not departed from your laws, for you yourself have taught me. 103 How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! 104 I gain understanding from your precepts; therefore I hate every wrong path. נ Nun 105 Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.

1 Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. 2 After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. 3 The tempter came to him and said, “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” 4 Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”

story: Last week we learned how to talk with our Father in prayer. This week we learn how our Father talks with us. He has given us the Bible, and the Bible is God’s Word.

Paul told Timothy to continue in what he had learned from the Holy Scriptures, “which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Then he said, “All Scripture is God-breathed.” That means the words of the Bible come from God. They are useful for teaching us, correcting us, and training us, so that we can be ready for every good work.

The psalm writer loved God’s law and thought about it all day long. He said, “Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.” In the dark, a lamp shows you where to step next. God does not leave us to guess our way through life. He lights the path with his Word.

When Jesus was hungry in the wilderness, the devil told him to turn stones into bread. Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” Jesus himself lived on God’s Word. He used what was written to stand against temptation.

So this is what we believe, and what we want to practice in our house. The Bible is God’s Word — God-breathed, a lamp for our feet, and the food we live on. We hide it in our hearts, we ask God to open our eyes, and we talk about it when we sit at home and when we walk along the road. The word of the Lord endures forever.
weeks.enochLine: The Bible is God’s Word. He talks to us here!
enochActivities: Activity: God’s book. Open a Bible, let Enoch touch the page, and say together, “This is God’s Word. He talks to us here!”
Activity: The lamp. Shine a flashlight at Enoch’s feet, take a few steps, and say, “Your Word is a lamp for my feet!”
elijahQuestions: In 2 Timothy 3:16, what does it say all Scripture is?
In Psalm 119:105, what is God’s word compared to?
In Matthew 4:4, what did Jesus say we must live on, not bread alone?
In 2 Timothy 3:15, what are the Holy Scriptures able to make you wise for?
jordynQuestions: Paul says all Scripture is “God-breathed” and also “useful” (2 Timothy 3:16–17). What is the Bible for, if it is more than a book of extra facts?
The psalm says, “Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long” (Psalm 119:97), and then, “Your word is a lamp for my feet” (verse 105). How do those two things go together?
Jesus was hungry, and the tempter told him to turn stones into bread (Matthew 4:2–4). Why does it matter that Jesus answered, “It is written”?
weeks.jordynApplication: The Bible is God’s Word: God-breathed, a lamp, and the food we live on (2 Timothy 3:16; Psalm 119:105; Matthew 4:4). This week, hide one verse in your heart, and use “It is written” when you are tempted. Talk about God’s Word at home, not only on Sunday (Deuteronomy 6:6–7).
elijahAnswers: “God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16). It is also useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness.
“A lamp for my feet, a light on my path” (Psalm 119:105).
“Every word that comes from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).
“Salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 3:15).
jordynAnswers: God gave the Scriptures to make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ, and to thoroughly equip us for every good work (2 Timothy 3:15–17). The Bible comes from God, leads us to Jesus, and trains us to live.
A lamp helps when you keep it with you and look at where it shines. Loving and meditating on God’s law all day is how the Word stays close enough to light the next step (Psalm 119:97, 105).

Jesus trusted his Father and used Scripture as his food and his answer. Real life comes from every word that comes from the mouth of God, not from grabbing bread in a way that doubts the Father (Matthew 4:1–4).
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she hid a verse in her heart, or used God’s Word when she was tempted. If it is fitting, share one way you lived on God’s Word too, and pray together that God would open your eyes.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that all Scripture is God-breathed, and that it can make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. Your word is a lamp for our feet. Teach us not to live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from your mouth. Open our eyes, and help us hide your Word in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: The Bible is God’s Word. All Scripture is God-breathed, and it can make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
dailies.verse: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness,
dailies.enoch: Hold a Bible close and say, “This is God’s Word. He talks to us here!”
dailies.elijah: In 2 Timothy 3:16, what does it say all Scripture is?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “God-breathed” (verse 16). It is also useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting, and training in righteousness.
dailies.jordyn: Verse 15 says the Holy Scriptures “are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” What is the Bible for, if it is more than a book of extra facts?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God gave the Scriptures to make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ, and to thoroughly equip us for every good work (verses 15–17). The Bible is God’s Word that leads us to Jesus and trains us to live.
dailies.action: Read 2 Timothy 3:14–17 together. Then each person thanks God for one person who has taught them the Scriptures, like Timothy had from infancy.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that all Scripture is God-breathed. Thank you that it can make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and that it can equip us for every good work. Help us continue in what we have learned. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we heard that the Bible is God’s Word. Paul told Timothy to continue in what he had learned, “because you know those from whom you learned it, and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.” Then he said, “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.” God-breathed means these words come from God. The Bible is not just a wise book people wrote on their own. It is God talking to us, to bring us to Jesus and to train us to live.
dailies.enochActivity: Open a Bible together. Let Enoch touch the page and say, “God-breathed. This is God’s Word!” Then a hug, because God talks to our family here.
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 17, what is the servant of God thoroughly equipped for?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Every good work” (verse 17).
dailies.jordyn2: Paul tells Timothy to “continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of” (verse 14). Why does “continue” matter, if Timothy has already known the Scriptures from infancy?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Knowing the Bible as a child is a gift, but we still need to keep going in it (verses 14–15). The Scriptures keep making us wise for salvation and keep equipping us. We do not graduate from God’s Word.
dailies.passageText: 14 But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned it, 15 and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: We hide God’s Word in our hearts. A young person stays on the path of purity by living according to God’s Word.
dailies.verse: I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you.
dailies.enoch: Pretend to tuck a small “word” card into your heart and say, “I hide your Word in my heart!”
dailies.elijah: In Psalm 119:11, where has the writer hidden God’s word, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “In my heart,” “that I might not sin against you” (verse 11).
dailies.jordyn: Verse 9 asks, “How can a young person stay on the path of purity?” What answer does the psalm give, and how does hiding the Word in the heart (verse 11) belong with that?
dailies.jordynAnswer: A young person stays on the path of purity “by living according to your word” (verse 9). Hiding the Word in the heart is how that Word is kept close, so we can live it and not sin against God (verses 9–11).
dailies.action: Play the hide-the-word game once, then read Psalm 119:9–11. Each person says one verse from this week they want to hide in their heart.
dailies.prayer: LORD, teach us your decrees. We want to hide your word in our hearts that we might not sin against you. Help us live according to your word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Bible is not only a book we hear on Sunday. The psalm asks, “How can a young person stay on the path of purity? By living according to your word.” Then it says, “I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you.” Hiding God’s Word does not mean we bury it and forget it. It means we keep it inside us, the way you keep a treasure in a safe place, so it can help us when we are tempted. The same psalm says, “I rejoice in following your statutes as one rejoices in great riches,” and “I will not neglect your word.” God’s Word is a treasure worth hiding, and a path worth walking.
dailies.enochActivity: Game: Hide the Word. Hide a small card with Psalm 119:11 in a room. When Enoch finds it, hold it to his chest and say together, “I have hidden your word in my heart!”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 16, what does the writer say he will not do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “I will not neglect your word” (verse 16).
dailies.jordyn2: The psalm says, “I rejoice in following your statutes as one rejoices in great riches” (verse 14). How is that different from treating the Bible as a rule book you only pick up when you are in trouble?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The writer delights in God’s Word and hides it in the heart before the moment of temptation (verses 11, 14–16). Living according to the Word is a joy and a treasure, not only an emergency tool.
dailies.passageText: 9 How can a young person stay on the path of purity? By living according to your word. 10 I seek you with all my heart; do not let me stray from your commands. 11 I have hidden your word in my heart that I might not sin against you. 12 Praise be to you, LORD; teach me your decrees. 13 With my lips I recount all the laws that come from your mouth. 14 I rejoice in following your statutes as one rejoices in great riches. 15 I meditate on your precepts and consider your ways. 16 I delight in your decrees; I will not neglect your word.

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: God’s Word is a lamp for our feet and a light on our path. We love his law and meditate on it, because it shows us where to walk.
dailies.verse: Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.
dailies.enoch: Shine a flashlight on the floor and take a few steps. Say, “Your Word is a lamp for my feet!”
dailies.elijah: In Psalm 119:105, what is God’s word compared to?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “A lamp for my feet, a light on my path” (verse 105).
dailies.jordyn: The psalm says, “Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long” (verse 97). How does loving and meditating on God’s Word go with the lamp in verse 105?
dailies.jordynAnswer: A lamp only helps if you keep it with you and look at where it shines. Loving and meditating on God’s law all day long is how the Word stays close enough to light the next step (verses 97, 105).
dailies.action: Read Psalm 119:97 and 119:105 together. Then walk a short path in the house with a flashlight, and thank God that his Word shows us where to go.
dailies.prayer: Father, we love your law. Your word is a lamp for our feet and a light on our path. Help us meditate on it and walk in it today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we heard, “Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.” A lamp in the dark does not always show the whole road at once. It shows the next steps, so you do not stumble. That is one reason the writer says, “Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long.” God’s Word stays with him: “Your commands are always with me.” He has more understanding because he obeys, and he does not turn aside from God’s laws. We do not guess our way through life in the dark. God has given us his Word to light the path.
dailies.enochActivity: Lamp walk: turn down the lights, shine a flashlight at Enoch’s feet, and take slow steps together. At the end say, “Your Word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path!”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 97, what does the writer say he does with God’s law all day long?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He meditates on it all day long (verse 97). He also says, “Oh, how I love your law!”
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 101 says, “I have kept my feet from every evil path so that I might obey your word.” How does that fit with the Bible being a lamp, not only a book we admire?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The light is for walking. The writer keeps his feet from evil paths so he can obey (verses 101, 105). God’s Word is meant to be lived, not only liked.
dailies.passageText: 97 Oh, how I love your law! I meditate on it all day long. 98 Your commands are always with me and make me wiser than my enemies. 99 I have more insight than all my teachers, for I meditate on your statutes. 100 I have more understanding than the elders, for I obey your precepts. 101 I have kept my feet from every evil path so that I might obey your word. 102 I have not departed from your laws, for you yourself have taught me. 103 How sweet are your words to my taste, sweeter than honey to my mouth! 104 I gain understanding from your precepts; therefore I hate every wrong path. נ Nun 105 Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path.

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: Jesus was hungry, and he still answered the devil with God’s Word: we do not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.
dailies.verse: Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”
dailies.enoch: Hold a piece of bread (or pretend), then hold a Bible, and say, “I need God’s Word more than bread!”
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 4:4, what did Jesus say we must live on, not bread alone?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Every word that comes from the mouth of God” (verse 4).
dailies.jordyn: Jesus was hungry after forty days and nights (verse 2). Why does it matter that he answered the tempter with “It is written,” instead of turning stones into bread?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus trusted his Father and used Scripture as his food and his answer (verses 1–4). He would not take a shortcut the devil offered, because real life comes from God’s Word, not from grabbing bread in a way that doubts the Father.
dailies.action: Read Matthew 4:1–4 twice. Then each person names one “bread” they are tempted to put first, and one word from God they will live on today.
dailies.prayer: Father, Jesus said we shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from your mouth. When we are hungry or tempted, help us answer with what is written, and trust you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. The tempter said, “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” Jesus did not argue from his hunger. He answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’” Today’s challenge is to treat God’s Word as food, not as an extra snack. We need bread, but we need the words that come from God’s mouth even more. When you are tempted this week, answer the way Jesus did: “It is written.”
dailies.enochActivity: Bread-and-Bible challenge: set a piece of bread beside an open Bible. Point to the bread, then to the Bible, and say Matthew 4:4 together: “Man shall not live on bread alone.”
dailies.elijah2: In verse 3, what did the tempter tell Jesus to turn the stones into?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Bread (verse 3).
dailies.jordyn2: How does “every word that comes from the mouth of God” (verse 4) fit with what we heard in 2 Timothy 3:16, that all Scripture is God-breathed?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Both teach that the words of Scripture come from God himself. That is why they can feed us and make us wise for salvation. Jesus lived by those words, and so do we (Matthew 4:4; 2 Timothy 3:16).
dailies.passageText: 1 Then Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil. 2 After fasting forty days and forty nights, he was hungry. 3 The tempter came to him and said, “If you are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread.” 4 Jesus answered, “It is written: ‘Man shall not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God.’”

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: We ask God to open our eyes in his Word, and we keep his commandments close — at home, on the road, when we lie down, and when we get up.
dailies.verse: Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in your law.
dailies.enoch: Cover your eyes, then open them, and pray, “Open my eyes, God. Help me see wonderful things in your Word.”
dailies.elijah: In Psalm 119:18, what does the writer ask God to open, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in your law” (Psalm 119:18).
dailies.jordyn: Deuteronomy 6:7 says to impress God’s commandments on your children, and to talk about them at home, on the road, at bedtime, and in the morning. Why is that more than a one-time Sunday reading?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God’s words are to be on our hearts all day, in ordinary moments, not only in a formal lesson (Deuteronomy 6:6–9). We need God to open our eyes (Psalm 119:18), and we also need a home that keeps talking about his Word.
dailies.action: Read Psalm 119:18 and Deuteronomy 6:6–7 together. Then pray, “Open my eyes,” and pick one ordinary time today (a meal, a walk, bedtime) to talk about a verse from this week.
dailies.prayer: Father, open our eyes that we may see wonderful things in your law. Put your commandments on our hearts. Help us talk about them when we sit at home and when we walk along the road, when we lie down and when we get up. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Because the Bible is God’s Word, we do not come to it as if we can see everything on our own. The psalm prays, “Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in your law.” That is a good prayer for every time we open the Bible. And Moses told God’s people not to leave those words in a book on a shelf: “These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up.” God’s Word belongs in the ordinary hours of a family.
dailies.enochActivity: Eyes-open prayer: cover eyes, then open them, and pray Psalm 119:18 one short phrase at a time. Then tape a verse card near a door and say, “We talk about God’s Word at home!”
dailies.elijah2: In Deuteronomy 6:7, when are we told to talk about God’s commandments?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “When you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (Deuteronomy 6:7).
dailies.jordyn2: Hebrews 4:12 says the word of God is “alive and active,” and that it “judges the thoughts and attitudes of the heart.” How does that fit with asking God to open our eyes in his law?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We need God to open our eyes because his Word is living; it does not only give information, it searches us (Psalm 119:18; Hebrews 4:12). We come to be taught, and also to be seen and changed.
dailies.passageText: 18 Open my eyes that I may see wonderful things in your law. 6 These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. 7 Impress them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up. 8 Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on your foreheads. 9 Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates.

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: The Bible is God’s Word — God-breathed, a lamp for our feet, and the food we live on. The word of our God endures forever.
dailies.verse: All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness,
dailies.enoch: Ask, “Whose Word is the Bible?” (God’s!) “What is God’s Word like?” (A lamp! Food! Forever!)
dailies.elijah: In 2 Timothy 3:16, what is all Scripture?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “God-breathed” (2 Timothy 3:16).
dailies.jordyn: This week we also heard that God’s Word is a lamp, and that Jesus lived on every word from God’s mouth. Why does a recap of “the Bible is God’s Word” need both the lamp and the food, not only “God-breathed”?
dailies.jordynAnswer: “God-breathed” tells us where the Bible comes from (2 Timothy 3:16). The lamp tells us it guides our steps (Psalm 119:105), and Jesus shows us we live by it (Matthew 4:4). We receive it as God’s Word, and we walk and eat by it.
dailies.action: Read 2 Timothy 3:16 and Psalm 119:105 together. Then each person shares one thing they learned this week and one way they want to keep God’s Word close.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that all Scripture is God-breathed, that your word is a lamp for our feet, and that we do not live on bread alone. The word of the Lord endures forever. Open our eyes, and help our family hide your Word in our hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week. All Scripture is God-breathed, able to make us wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus, and able to equip us for every good work. We hide God’s Word in our hearts. It is a lamp for our feet and a light on our path. Jesus would not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God. We ask God to open our eyes, and we talk about his commandments in the ordinary hours of the day. People are like grass, and flowers fall, “but the word of the Lord endures forever.” That is the Word that has been preached to us. We can trust it, love it, and live by it.
dailies.enochActivity: Recap motions: hold a Bible (“God-breathed”), shine a light at your feet (“a lamp”), and take a bite of air like food (“every word”). Then say, “The Bible is God’s Word!”
dailies.elijah2: In Psalm 119:105, what is God’s word for our feet and our path?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “A lamp for my feet, a light on my path” (Psalm 119:105).
dailies.jordyn2: 1 Peter 1:24–25 says people are like grass, but “the word of the Lord endures forever.” How does that change the way a family treats the Bible compared with other words that come and go?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Other words fade, like flowers. God’s Word remains, and it is the word that was preached to us (1 Peter 1:23–25). So we keep returning to it, not treating it as one more passing voice.
dailies.passageText: 16 All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness, 17 so that the servant of God may be thoroughly equipped for every good work. Your word is a lamp for my feet, a light on my path. For, “All people are like grass, and all their glory is like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord endures forever.” And this is the word that was preached to you.

weeks.planTitle: God's design for marriage and family
weeks.title: God's design for marriage and family
weeks.selectLabel: Week 17 · God's design for marriage and family
weeks.nextUp: Week 18 · Loving everyone made in God's image
weeks.bigIdea: God made marriage: a husband and a wife, joined by God as one. Children honor their father and mother. Fathers bring their children up in the Lord, and husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 17 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Genesis 2:18–24 out loud, then Matthew 19:4–6, then Ephesians 5:25, 31–33 and 6:1–4.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 18 The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper suitable for him.” 19 Now the LORD God had formed out of the ground all the wild animals and all the birds in the sky. He brought them to the man to see what he would name them; and whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. 20 So the man gave names to all the livestock, the birds in the sky and all the wild animals. But for Adam no suitable helper was found. 21 So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep; and while he was sleeping, he took one of the man’s ribs and then closed up the place with flesh. 22 Then the LORD God made a woman from the rib he had taken out of the man, and he brought her to the man. 23 The man said, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for she was taken out of man.” 24 That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.

4 “Haven’t you read,” he replied, “that at the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ 5 and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”

25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 31 “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” 32 This is a profound mystery—but I am talking about Christ and the church. 33 However, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband. 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise— 3 “so that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.” 4 Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

story: Last week we learned that the Bible is God’s Word. This week we listen to what that Word says about marriage and family. These things are God’s idea, not something people made up later.

In the beginning, the LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” He made a woman, a helper suitable for the man, and brought her to him. The man was glad. “That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.” God joined a husband and a wife into one new family.

When people tested Jesus about marriage, he took them back to that beginning. The Creator “made them male and female.” A man is united to his wife, and the two become one flesh. “So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” Marriage is a joining God does, and we are not to pull it apart.

God also gave a word to children and to parents. “Honor your father and your mother.” “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.” And fathers are told not to exasperate their children, but to bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. Husbands are told to love their wives “just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.”

So this is God’s design, and it is a gift. A husband and a wife belong to each other for life. Children honor father and mother. Parents train their children in the Lord with love, not harshness. Children are a heritage from the LORD. We want our house to look like that design.
weeks.enochLine: God made our family. I can honor Mom and Dad!
enochActivities: Activity: God made them one. Join two hands together and say, “God made a husband and a wife one family!”
Activity: Honor hug. Give Mom and Dad a hug and say, “I honor you!”
elijahQuestions: In Genesis 2:18, what did the LORD God say was not good?
In Genesis 2:24, what happens when a man is united to his wife?
In Matthew 19:6, what does Jesus say no one should do to what God has joined together?
In Ephesians 6:1, what are children told to do?
jordynQuestions: Genesis 2:24 says a husband and wife become “one flesh.” Jesus adds, “What God has joined together, let no one separate” (Matthew 19:6). What is God doing in a marriage, if this is more than two people only living under one roof?
Ephesians 6:1–4 speaks to children and to fathers. Why does God’s design for a family need both of those words, not only the command for children?
Husbands are told to love their wives “just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25). What kind of love is that, compared with a love that only wants to be served?
weeks.jordynApplication: God made marriage, and he joins a husband and wife for life (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:6). This week, honor your father and mother in a concrete way, and notice how the adults in your house are called to love like Christ, not harshly (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 5:25; 6:1–4).
elijahAnswers: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (Genesis 2:18). He said he would make “a helper suitable for him.”
“They become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). He leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife.
“Let no one separate” (Matthew 19:6). They are “no longer two, but one flesh.”
“Obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (Ephesians 6:1).
jordynAnswers: God himself joins a husband and wife into one new family for life (Genesis 2:18–24; Matthew 19:4–6). Marriage is his design and his joining, not a thin arrangement people may break when they wish.

Children are to obey and honor, and fathers must not exasperate their children, but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord (Ephesians 6:1–4). A holy family is not only well-behaved children. It is also parents who train without crushing.

It is a self-giving love, like Christ’s: he gave himself up for the church (Ephesians 5:25). A husband is called to spend himself for his wife’s good, not to be harsh or to live as if the home exists only to serve him.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she practiced honoring father or mother in a concrete way, and whether she saw something of Christ’s kind of love at home. If it is fitting, share one way you honored God’s design this week too, and pray together for your family.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that it is not good for us to be alone, and that you made marriage — a husband and a wife, joined by you as one. What you have joined together, let no one separate. Help our children honor father and mother, and help the parents in this house bring the children up in the Lord with love, not harshness. Teach husbands to love as Christ loved the church. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2
dailies.focus: God saw that it was not good for the man to be alone. He made a wife for him, and the two became one family.
dailies.verse: That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.
dailies.enoch: Hold a parent’s hand and say, “God made families! It is not good to be all alone.”
dailies.elijah: In Genesis 2:18, what did the LORD God say was not good?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “It is not good for the man to be alone” (verse 18). He said he would make “a helper suitable for him.”
dailies.jordyn: Verse 24 says a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become “one flesh.” What is God doing in a marriage, if this is more than two people only living in the same house?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God joins a husband and wife into one new family for life (verses 18, 22–24). The wife is a “helper suitable” — a partner who corresponds to him, not a leftover. Marriage is God’s idea, not a human invention.
dailies.action: Read Genesis 2:18 and 2:24 together. Then thank God for one way he has given your family to one another, so no one has to be alone.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that it is not good for us to be alone, and that you made marriage and family. Thank you that a husband and wife can be united and become one. Help our home honor your design. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: On Sunday we heard that God made marriage. The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper suitable for him.” After Adam named the animals, no suitable helper was found. So the LORD God made a woman, and brought her to the man. The man said she was “bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.” “That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.” God did not leave people to invent marriage. He made a husband and a wife to belong to each other, and to start a new family together.
dailies.enochActivity: Pair-up: two parents stand a step apart, then join hands and say, “God made them one family!” Let Enoch stand close and say, “God made our family too!”
dailies.elijah2: Find it in the passage: In verse 23, what did the man say about the woman?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for she was taken out of man” (verse 23).
dailies.jordyn2: The woman is called a “helper suitable for him” (verse 18). How does that fit with the man also calling her bone of his bones, not a servant he named like the animals?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The animals were named, but none was a suitable helper (verses 19–20). The woman is from his side, brought to him by God, and they become one (verses 22–24). “Helper” here means a partner who corresponds to him, standing with him.
dailies.passageText: 18 The LORD God said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make a helper suitable for him.” 19 Now the LORD God had formed out of the ground all the wild animals and all the birds in the sky. He brought them to the man to see what he would name them; and whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. 20 So the man gave names to all the livestock, the birds in the sky and all the wild animals. But for Adam no suitable helper was found. 21 So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep; and while he was sleeping, he took one of the man’s ribs and then closed up the place with flesh. 22 Then the LORD God made a woman from the rib he had taken out of the man, and he brought her to the man. 23 The man said, “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for she was taken out of man.” 24 That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.

dailies.label: Day 3
dailies.focus: God’s design for family includes this command: honor your father and your mother.
dailies.verse: Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.
dailies.enoch: Give a parent a hug and say, “I honor you! Thank you, Mom. Thank you, Dad.”
dailies.elijah: In Exodus 20:12, whom are we told to honor?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12).
dailies.jordyn: The command comes with a promise: “so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.” What does that tell you about honoring parents, if it is more than only saying “yes” once?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Honoring father and mother is part of the life God wants for his people in the land he gives (Exodus 20:12). It is a way of life, not a one-time word, and God attaches a promise to it.
dailies.action: Play the honor game once, then read Exodus 20:12. Each child does one real honor-task for a parent today, without being asked twice.
dailies.prayer: LORD, you told us to honor our father and our mother. Thank you for the parents you have given us. Help us honor them in our words and in our work today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God’s design for family is not only about a wedding. He also told his people, “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.” Honor means we treat Mom and Dad as gifts from God. We speak to them with respect. We listen. We help. We do not mock them or drag our feet when they lead our home in what is right. This command has a promise with it, because a home that honors father and mother is a home God meant to be a blessing.
dailies.enochActivity: Game: Honor helpers. A parent names a simple job (a toy to put away, a shoe to bring). Enoch runs to do it with a smile and says, “I honor you!” Then a hug.
dailies.elijah2: In Exodus 20:12, what promise is given with the command to honor father and mother?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “So that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you” (Exodus 20:12).
dailies.jordyn2: How does honoring father and mother fit with last week, when we heard that God’s Word should be on our hearts and talked about at home (Deuteronomy 6:6–7)?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Parents are to impress God’s commandments on their children at home. Children honor father and mother by receiving that teaching and treating them with respect (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 6:6–7). Both belong to God’s design for a family.
dailies.passageText: 12 “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.

dailies.label: Day 4
dailies.focus: Jesus takes us back to the beginning. God made them male and female, and what God has joined together, no one should separate.
dailies.verse: So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.
dailies.enoch: Hold two hands together tightly and say, “What God joins, we do not pull apart!”
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 19:6, what does Jesus say no one should do to what God has joined together?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Let no one separate” (verse 6). He says they are “no longer two, but one flesh.”
dailies.jordyn: Jesus answers a question about marriage by saying, “Haven’t you read,” and then quoting Genesis (verses 4–5). Why does he take people back to “the beginning” instead of starting with what is easy or popular?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus treats God’s design at creation as the rule for marriage: the Creator made them male and female, and a man is united to his wife (verses 4–6). Marriage is what God has joined, not only what people feel like doing at the moment.
dailies.action: Read Matthew 19:4–6 together. Then thank God that he joins a husband and wife, and pray for one married couple you know to stay faithful.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that at the beginning you made them male and female, and that a husband and wife become one flesh. What you have joined together, let no one separate. Help us honor marriage in our family. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Some people came to Jesus to test him about marriage. He did not start with their test. He said, “Haven’t you read that at the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” Jesus agrees with Genesis. Marriage is God’s joining of a man and a woman for life. We do not treat it as a thin promise we can break when we are tired of it.
dailies.enochActivity: Join-and-hold: hook two fingers together (or two hands) and try, gently, not to pull them apart. Say, “What God has joined together, let no one separate.”
dailies.elijah2: In Matthew 19:4, whom did the Creator make at the beginning?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He “made them male and female” (verse 4).
dailies.jordyn2: Jesus says they are “no longer two, but one flesh” (verse 6). How does that help you understand Genesis 2:24, which we read on Day 2?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Jesus is reading Genesis 2:24 as God’s own work. The leaving and uniting is not only a couple’s choice; it is what God has joined, and no one should separate it (Matthew 19:4–6).
dailies.passageText: 4 “Haven’t you read,” he replied, “that at the beginning the Creator ‘made them male and female,’ 5 and said, ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh’? 6 So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.”

dailies.label: Day 5
dailies.focus: Children, obey your parents in the Lord. Fathers, bring your children up in the training and instruction of the Lord, not by making them bitter.
dailies.verse: Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.
dailies.enoch: When a parent gives a kind instruction, practice a quick “Yes!” and then do it.
dailies.elijah: In Ephesians 6:1, what are children told to do, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (verse 1).
dailies.jordyn: Verses 2–3 repeat “Honor your father and mother” and call it “the first commandment with a promise.” How is honoring bigger than only obeying a single instruction?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Obeying is doing what parents ask in the Lord (verse 1). Honoring is the deeper posture of respect that goes with it, and God attaches a promise to it (verses 2–3). A child can do a task and still dishonor a parent with the face or the tone.
dailies.action: Read Ephesians 6:1–4 twice. Children: name one way you will obey and honor today. Parents: name one way you will bring the children up in the Lord’s instruction, without exasperate-and-scold only.
dailies.prayer: Father, help the children in this house obey their parents in the Lord, and to honor father and mother. Help the fathers, and all of us who lead, not to exasperate our children, but to bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul takes the fifth commandment into a Christian home. “Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right.” “Honor your father and mother”—which, he says, is the first commandment with a promise: “so that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.” Then he turns to fathers: “Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.” God’s design has a word for children and a word for dads. Children obey and honor. Fathers do not crush their children; they raise them in the Lord’s ways. Today’s challenge is to practice both sides of that design.
dailies.enochActivity: Yes-and-do: a parent gives one short, kind instruction. Enoch says, “Yes!” and does it. Then the parent says, “Thank you. We train you in the Lord with love.”
dailies.elijah2: In Ephesians 6:4, what are fathers told not to do, and what should they do instead?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord” (verse 4).
dailies.jordyn2: Why does a lesson on God’s design for family need verse 4, and not only the command for children in verses 1–3?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Parents can be right about the rule and still exasperate a child (verse 4). God’s design is not only a child’s obedience. It is a father’s careful training in the Lord, so the home is not harsh and empty of the Lord’s instruction.
dailies.passageText: 1 Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right. 2 “Honor your father and mother”—which is the first commandment with a promise— 3 “so that it may go well with you and that you may enjoy long life on the earth.” 4 Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord.

dailies.label: Day 6
dailies.focus: We pray for our home: husbands love, families do not turn bitter, and we receive children as a heritage from the LORD.
dailies.verse: Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and pray, “Thank you, God, for Mom and Dad. Help us love one another.”
dailies.elijah: In Ephesians 5:25, how are husbands told to love their wives?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (Ephesians 5:25).
dailies.jordyn: Colossians 3:19 says, “Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them,” and 3:21 says, “Fathers, do not embitter your children.” What kind of home is God designing, if love is more than a feeling?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God’s design is a home where the husband’s love looks like Christ’s self-giving, not harshness, and where children are not embittered (Ephesians 5:25; Colossians 3:19, 21). Love here is how we treat one another, including when we pray.
dailies.action: Read Ephesians 5:25 and Psalm 127:3 together. Then let each person pray one short sentence for Mom, for Dad, or for the children of the house.
dailies.prayer: Father, help the husbands in your church love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her. Help our family not be harsh or bitter. Thank you that children are a heritage from the LORD. Teach us to love one another in this house. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: God’s design for a family is full of love that looks like Jesus. “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her.” In a short household word, Paul also says, “Wives, submit yourselves to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them. Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord. Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged.” And the psalm reminds us why children are not a burden only: “Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him.” Today we pray those words over our house.
dailies.enochActivity: Family-pray: sit close, fold hands, and thank God for each person by name. End with, “Children are a heritage from the LORD.”
dailies.elijah2: In Psalm 127:3, what are children called?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “A heritage from the LORD,” and “offspring a reward from him” (Psalm 127:3).
dailies.jordyn2: How does a husband’s love “as Christ loved the church” (Ephesians 5:25) protect a home from the harshness and embitterment Colossians 3 warns against?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Christ gave himself up for the church. That kind of love does not treat a wife harshly or crush children until they are discouraged (Ephesians 5:25; Colossians 3:19, 21). It spends itself for their good.
dailies.passageText: 25 Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her 18 Wives, submit yourselves to your husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. 19 Husbands, love your wives and do not be harsh with them. 20 Children, obey your parents in everything, for this pleases the Lord. 21 Fathers, do not embitter your children, or they will become discouraged. Children are a heritage from the LORD, offspring a reward from him.

dailies.label: Day 7
dailies.focus: Recap: God made marriage — a husband and wife joined as one. Children honor father and mother. What God has joined together, let no one separate.
dailies.verse: That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh.
dailies.enoch: Ask, “Who made marriage?” (God!) “What do children do?” (Honor father and mother!)
dailies.elijah: In Genesis 2:24, what happens when a man is united to his wife?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “They become one flesh” (Genesis 2:24). He leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife.
dailies.jordyn: This week we also heard Jesus say, “What God has joined together, let no one separate,” and Paul tell children to obey and fathers not to exasperate. Why does a recap of “God’s design for marriage and family” need both the joining and the honoring?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Marriage is God’s joining of a husband and wife for life (Genesis 2:24; Matthew 19:6). A family also needs children who honor father and mother, and fathers who bring children up in the Lord without crushing them (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:1–4). Both are God’s design.
dailies.action: Read Genesis 2:24 and Matthew 19:6 together. Then each person shares one thing they learned this week and one way they will honor God’s design at home.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you made marriage, and that what you have joined together no one should separate. Help us honor father and mother, love one another like Christ, and receive our family as a gift from you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Today we look back at our week. The LORD God said it was not good for the man to be alone, and he made a wife, a helper suitable for him. A man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. Jesus said the Creator made them male and female, and “what God has joined together, let no one separate.” God also said, “Honor your father and your mother.” Children obey their parents in the Lord; fathers do not exasperate their children, but bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. Husbands love their wives as Christ loved the church. Children are a heritage from the LORD. That is God’s design for marriage and family, and we want to live it in this house.
dailies.enochActivity: Recap motions: join two hands (“God makes them one”), hug a parent (“Honor father and mother”), and say, “What God joins, we do not pull apart!”
dailies.elijah2: In Matthew 19:6, what does Jesus say about what God has joined together?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Let no one separate” (Matthew 19:6).
dailies.jordyn2: Ephesians 5:25 tells husbands to love as Christ loved the church. How does that belong in a recap that also includes “honor your father and mother”?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God’s design is a whole house: a husband’s self-giving love, a marriage God has joined, and children who honor their parents (Ephesians 5:25; Matthew 19:6; Exodus 20:12). Each part helps the others.
dailies.passageText: That is why a man leaves his father and mother and is united to his wife, and they become one flesh. So they are no longer two, but one flesh. Therefore what God has joined together, let no one separate.” 12 “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long in the land the LORD your God is giving you.

weeks.planTitle: Loving everyone made in God's image
weeks.title: Loving everyone made in God's image
weeks.selectLabel: Week 18 · Loving everyone made in God's image
weeks.nextUp: Week 19 · Heaven: our forever home
weeks.bigIdea: God made every person in his image. We love our neighbor as ourselves — without picking favorites — because every person bears that image.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 18 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Genesis 1:26–27 out loud, then Luke 10:25–37, then James 2:1–9.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 26 Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” 27 So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.

25 On one occasion an expert in the law stood up to test Jesus. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 26 “What is written in the Law?” he replied. “How do you read it?” 27 He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’; and, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” 28 “You have answered correctly,” Jesus replied. “Do this and you will live.” 29 But he wanted to justify himself, so he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” 30 In reply Jesus said: “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, when he was attacked by robbers. They stripped him of his clothes, beat him and went away, leaving him half dead. 31 A priest happened to be going down the same road, and when he saw the man, he passed by on the other side. 32 So too, a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. 33 But a Samaritan, as he traveled, came where the man was; and when he saw him, he took pity on him. 34 He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put the man on his own donkey, brought him to an inn and took care of him. 35 The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Look after him,’ he said, ‘and when I return, I will reimburse you for any extra expense you may have.’ 36 “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” 37 The expert in the law replied, “The one who had mercy on him.” Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”

1 My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism. 2 Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in filthy old clothes also comes in. 3 If you show special attention to the man wearing fine clothes and say, “Here’s a good seat for you,” but say to the poor man, “You stand there” or “Sit on the floor by my feet,” 4 have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? 5 Listen, my dear brothers and sisters: Has not God chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised those who love him? 6 But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who are exploiting you? Are they not the ones who are dragging you into court? 7 Are they not the ones who are blaspheming the noble name of him to whom you belong? 8 If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing right. 9 But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.

story: Last week we learned God’s design for marriage and family. This week we look wider. In Week 1 we heard that God made people in his image. Today we learn what that means for how we treat everyone.

“Then God said, ‘Let us make mankind in our image.’” “So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.” Every person you meet is made in God’s image — not only people who look like you, or like you, or can do what you can do.

An expert in the law asked Jesus what he must do to inherit eternal life. Jesus pointed him back to the Law: love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself. The man wanted to justify himself. “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus told of a man who was beaten and left hurt on the road. A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side. A Samaritan — someone the hearers did not expect to honor — stopped, took pity, bandaged the wounds, and paid for his care. “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor?” “The one who had mercy on him.” Jesus said, “Go and do likewise.”

James says the same love must show up when people walk into the room. Believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism — a good seat for the person in fine clothes, and “sit on the floor” for the poor. “If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin.”
So this is the word for our house: God made every person in his image. Love God. Love your neighbor as yourself. Do not pick favorites. Go and do likewise.
weeks.enochLine: God made every person. I can be kind to everyone!
enochActivities: Activity: Image of God. Look at each person in the room, point gently, and say, “God made you in his image!”
Activity: Neighbor help. With a grown-up, put a bandage on a stuffed animal or doll and say, “I can stop and help.”
elijahQuestions: In Genesis 1:26, in whose image did God want to make mankind?
In Luke 10:27, whom are we told to love as ourselves?
In Luke 10:33–34, who stopped and helped the hurt man?
In James 2:1, what must believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ not show?
jordynQuestions: Genesis 1:27 says God created mankind in his own image. How should that change the way you treat a person you find hard to like, or a person who cannot do what you can do?
In Luke 10, Jesus makes the neighbor a Samaritan — someone the hearers did not expect to honor — while a priest and a Levite pass by. What is Jesus teaching about “who is my neighbor”?
James 2:1–9 warns against a good seat for the person in fine clothes and “sit on the floor” for the poor. How is favoritism a failure to keep the royal law, “Love your neighbor as yourself”?
weeks.jordynApplication: Every person is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). This week, love your neighbor as yourself in a concrete way: notice someone easy to overlook, and honor them as an image-bearer, without favoritism (Luke 10:36–37; James 2:1, 8).
elijahAnswers: In “our image” — God’s image (Genesis 1:26). “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness.”
“Your neighbor” (Luke 10:27). We are also told to love the Lord our God with all our heart, soul, strength, and mind.
A Samaritan. “When he saw him, he took pity on him.” He bandaged his wounds and took care of him (Luke 10:33–34).
Favoritism. “Believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism” (James 2:1).
jordynAnswers: That person is made in God’s image too (Genesis 1:26–27). Their worth does not come from whether they are easy, impressive, or like us. We treat them with the dignity God gave them.
Your neighbor is not only your friend or your people. The neighbor is the one who needs mercy, even someone you might pass by or look down on. Jesus says, “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:29–37).

Favoritism honors the impressive and dishonors the poor, and James says that is sin (James 2:1–9). The royal law loves the neighbor as yourself — not only the neighbor who can give you something back.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she practiced loving a neighbor in a concrete way, especially someone easy to overlook, and whether she refused favoritism. If it is fitting, share one way you honored an image-bearer this week too, and pray together.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you made mankind in your image — every person, male and female. Teach us to love you with all our heart, and to love our neighbor as ourselves. Keep us from favoritism. Make us like the one who had mercy, and help us go and do likewise. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: God made mankind in his own image. Every person bears that image.
dailies.verse: So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
dailies.enoch: Look at each person in the room and say, “God made you!”
dailies.elijah: In Genesis 1:27, in whose image did God create mankind?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “In his own image,” “in the image of God.” He created them “male and female.”
dailies.jordyn: If every person is made in God’s image, what is wrong with treating some people as if they matter less?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Their worth comes from the God who made them in his image (Genesis 1:26–27), not from how useful, likeable, or impressive they seem to us. To treat someone as less is to forget who made them.
dailies.action: Name one person you will treat today as someone made in God’s image — especially someone easy to rush past.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you made us in your image. Help us see every person that way today. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: In the beginning, God made mankind on purpose, in his image and likeness — male and female. That is why every person has God-given dignity. This week we will learn what that means for how we love our neighbor.
dailies.enochActivity: Point to your own face in a mirror, then to a family member, and say, “God made us in his image!”
dailies.elijah2: In Genesis 1:26, what job did God give the people he made in his image?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: To “rule over” the fish, birds, livestock, wild animals, and creatures that move along the ground — to care for his world (Genesis 1:26).
dailies.jordyn2: Week 1 taught that God made you in his image. This week asks how that same truth should shape the way you treat everyone else. What is the difference?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: It is not only about my own worth. It is about my neighbor’s worth too. If God made them in his image, I am not free to ignore, mock, or rank them as if they were less (Genesis 1:26–27).
dailies.passageText: 26 Then God said, “Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness, so that they may rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky, over the livestock and all the wild animals, and over all the creatures that move along the ground.” 27 So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Jesus names two great commands: love God, and love your neighbor as yourself.
dailies.verse: And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’
dailies.enoch: Hold up one finger and say, “Love God!” Hold up two fingers and say, “Love my neighbor!”
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 22:37–38, what does Jesus call the first and greatest commandment?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.” That is the first and greatest commandment.
dailies.jordyn: Jesus says the second command is “like” the first: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” How is loving your neighbor connected to loving God, not a separate leftover rule?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The neighbor is made in God’s image (Genesis 1:27). To love the Lord with all your heart, and then treat his image-bearers as if they do not matter, is not whole love. The second command is like the first because the people we love belong to the God we love.
dailies.action: Play the two-finger game once at a meal: a grown-up names a moment from the day, and everyone holds up one finger (love God) or two (love neighbor) and says how they could do it.
dailies.prayer: Lord, help us love you with all our heart, and love our neighbor as ourselves. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus was asked about the greatest commandment. He did not give only one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, and mind — that is first. And the second is like it: love your neighbor as yourself. Both belong together.
dailies.enochActivity: Practice the game: a grown-up says “Love God” or “Love your neighbor,” and you hold up one finger or two and smile.
dailies.elijah2: In Matthew 22:39, whom are we told to love as ourselves?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Your neighbor.” “And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’”
dailies.jordyn2: What is one concrete way “love your neighbor as yourself” could look in your house or at school tomorrow, not only as a phrase you can recite?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: sharing, including someone left out, speaking kindly, helping without being asked. The command is not only words. It is how you treat a real person made in God’s image.
dailies.passageText: 37 Jesus replied: “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind.’ 38 This is the first and greatest commandment. 39 And the second is like it: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Jesus tells of a Samaritan who stopped to help. The neighbor is the one who shows mercy.
dailies.verse: The expert in the law replied, “The one who had mercy on him.” Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”
dailies.enoch: Act out stopping to help: kneel, pretend to bandage, and say, “I can help.”
dailies.elijah: In Luke 10:31–32, what did the priest and the Levite do when they saw the hurt man?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They “passed by on the other side.” They saw him and did not stop.
dailies.jordyn: The expert asked, “And who is my neighbor?” Jesus answers with a story, then asks who was a neighbor to the hurt man. How does that change the question?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The man wanted a list of who counts. Jesus asks who became a neighbor by showing mercy (Luke 10:29, 36–37). The question is not “Whom can I leave out?” It is “Will I go and do likewise?”
dailies.action: Do one concrete act of mercy today for someone who needs help, even a small one, without waiting to be asked.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, thank you for showing us what a neighbor looks like. Make us people who stop and have mercy. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: A man was beaten and left hurt on the road. A priest and a Levite passed by on the other side. A Samaritan took pity, bandaged his wounds, and paid for his care. Jesus asked who was a neighbor to the man. “The one who had mercy on him.” Then he said, “Go and do likewise.”
dailies.enochActivity: With a grown-up, help someone in the house in a small way (a toy put away, a hug, a drink of water) and say, “Go and do likewise.”
dailies.elijah2: In Luke 10:33–34, what did the Samaritan do when he saw the hurt man?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He “took pity on him.” He went to him, bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine, put him on his own donkey, brought him to an inn, and took care of him.
dailies.jordyn2: Why does it matter that the one who had mercy was a Samaritan, not the priest or the Levite?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The hearers did not expect a Samaritan to be the example. Jesus will not let us limit “neighbor” to our own people or to impressive religious people. Mercy can come from the one we might pass by — and we are called to show that mercy ourselves (Luke 10:33–37).
dailies.passageText: 25 On one occasion an expert in the law stood up to test Jesus. “Teacher,” he asked, “what must I do to inherit eternal life?” 26 “What is written in the Law?” he replied. “How do you read it?” 27 He answered, “‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength and with all your mind’; and, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” 28 “You have answered correctly,” Jesus replied. “Do this and you will live.” 29 But he wanted to justify himself, so he asked Jesus, “And who is my neighbor?” 30 In reply Jesus said: “A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, when he was attacked by robbers. They stripped him of his clothes, beat him and went away, leaving him half dead. 31 A priest happened to be going down the same road, and when he saw the man, he passed by on the other side. 32 So too, a Levite, when he came to the place and saw him, passed by on the other side. 33 But a Samaritan, as he traveled, came where the man was; and when he saw him, he took pity on him. 34 He went to him and bandaged his wounds, pouring on oil and wine. Then he put the man on his own donkey, brought him to an inn and took care of him. 35 The next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper. ‘Look after him,’ he said, ‘and when I return, I will reimburse you for any extra expense you may have.’ 36 “Which of these three do you think was a neighbor to the man who fell into the hands of robbers?” 37 The expert in the law replied, “The one who had mercy on him.” Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Believers in Jesus must not show favoritism. The royal law is to love your neighbor as yourself.
dailies.verse: My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism.
dailies.enoch: Practice giving the same kind welcome to two toys or two chairs: no “best seat” for only one. Say, “No favorites!”
dailies.elijah: In James 2:2–3, how is the man in fine clothes treated differently from the poor man?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The man in fine clothes is given “a good seat.” The poor man is told, “You stand there” or “Sit on the floor by my feet.”
dailies.jordyn: James says if you show favoritism you sin, even if you can recite “Love your neighbor as yourself.” Why is the royal law broken by a seating chart?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The royal law loves the neighbor as yourself (James 2:8–9). Favoritism honors the impressive and dishonors the poor. That is not love. It is judging with evil thoughts (James 2:4).
dailies.action: Challenge: at school, church, or home, honor someone who is usually overlooked. Do not give the “good seat” only to the impressive person.
dailies.prayer: Father, keep us from favoritism. Help us love our neighbor as ourselves, including the person who is easy to ignore. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: James is plain: believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism. A good seat for fine clothes, and the floor for the poor, is not love. “If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing right. But if you show favoritism, you sin.”
dailies.enochActivity: When you sit down to a meal, help a grown-up welcome everyone the same way: a smile and a kind word for each person.
dailies.elijah2: In James 2:8–9, what happens if you show favoritism?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “If you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.” The royal law is “Love your neighbor as yourself.”
dailies.jordyn2: Has not God chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith (James 2:5)? How should that change whose welcome you work hardest to give?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: God’s welcome does not follow fine clothes. If anything, James warns that dishonoring the poor is a serious wrong (James 2:5–6). Work hardest to honor the person who might be left standing.
dailies.passageText: 1 My brothers and sisters, believers in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ must not show favoritism. 2 Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in filthy old clothes also comes in. 3 If you show special attention to the man wearing fine clothes and say, “Here’s a good seat for you,” but say to the poor man, “You stand there” or “Sit on the floor by my feet,” 4 have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts? 5 Listen, my dear brothers and sisters: Has not God chosen those who are poor in the eyes of the world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom he promised those who love him? 6 But you have dishonored the poor. Is it not the rich who are exploiting you? Are they not the ones who are dragging you into court? 7 Are they not the ones who are blaspheming the noble name of him to whom you belong? 8 If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing right. 9 But if you show favoritism, you sin and are convicted by the law as lawbreakers.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: We love one another because love comes from God. He loved us first, and sent his Son.
dailies.verse: Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say, “God loves us. Help me love too.”
dailies.elijah: In 1 John 4:8, why does the one who does not love not know God?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Because God is love.” “Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love.”
