dailies.jordyn: 1 John 4:10 says, “This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.” How does that keep “love your neighbor” from becoming a way we try to earn God’s love?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Love starts with God, not with us. He loved us and sent his Son. We love one another because he so loved us (1 John 4:10–11), not in order to get him to love us.
dailies.action: Pray for one person who is hard to love, and ask God to help you show them kindness today.
dailies.prayer: Father, you are love. You loved us and sent your Son. Teach us to love one another, so that your love is made complete in us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Love comes from God. “Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God.” “God is love.” He showed his love by sending his Son. “Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.” We have not seen God, but if we love one another, God lives in us.
dailies.enochActivity: Give someone a hug or a kind word, then pray, “Thank you, God, for loving us.”
dailies.elijah2: In 1 John 4:9–10, how did God show his love among us?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him.” “He loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins.”
dailies.jordyn2: Verse 12 says, “No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us.” What does loving a real neighbor have to do with knowing the God we cannot see?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We cannot see God, but we can love the people made in his image. When we love one another, John says God lives in us and his love is made complete in us (1 John 4:12). Neighbor-love is not a side job. It is how his love shows.
dailies.passageText: 7 Dear friends, let us love one another, for love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. 8 Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. 9 This is how God showed his love among us: He sent his one and only Son into the world that we might live through him. 10 This is love: not that we loved God, but that he loved us and sent his Son as an atoning sacrifice for our sins. 11 Dear friends, since God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. 12 No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God lives in us and his love is made complete in us.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: God made every person in his image. Love your neighbor as yourself. Go and do likewise, without favoritism.
dailies.verse: So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them.
dailies.enoch: Say this week’s line out loud: “God made every person. I can be kind to everyone!”
dailies.elijah: Can you tell, in your own words, what the Samaritan did — and what Jesus said after the story?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Samaritan took pity, helped the hurt man, and took care of him. Jesus said the neighbor was “the one who had mercy on him,” and “Go and do likewise” (Luke 10:33–37).
dailies.jordyn: How do Genesis 1:27, Luke 10:37, and James 2:8 fit together as one week, not three separate lessons?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God made every person in his image (Genesis 1:27). Jesus commands us to go and show mercy like a true neighbor (Luke 10:37). James says that same royal law — love your neighbor as yourself — means no favoritism (James 2:8–9). Image, mercy, and fairness are one love.
dailies.action: Look back on the week: where did you love a neighbor well, and where did you show favoritism or pass by? Tell a grown-up one honest answer, and ask God for help for the week ahead.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for making us in your image. Help our family love you, love our neighbor, show mercy, and refuse favoritism. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that God made every person in his image. Jesus said to love your neighbor as yourself, and he told us to go and do likewise — like the one who had mercy. James said the royal law is that same love, and favoritism is sin. That is enough to live this week.
dailies.enochActivity: Draw three simple pictures with a grown-up: people God made, a helper stopping to help, and a kind welcome for everyone.
dailies.elijah2: In James 2:8, what is the royal law found in Scripture?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Love your neighbor as yourself.” If you really keep it, “you are doing right.”
dailies.jordyn2: Who is one image-bearer you are likely to pass by or rank lower next week, and what would “go and do likewise” look like with that person?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary. Be specific: a name, a hallway, a lunch table, a younger sibling. Mercy is not a story we only admire. It is a next step with a real person God made in his image.
dailies.passageText: So God created mankind in his own image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them. The expert in the law replied, “The one who had mercy on him.” Jesus told him, “Go and do likewise.” If you really keep the royal law found in Scripture, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” you are doing right.

weeks.title: Heaven: our forever home
weeks.selectLabel: Week 19 · Heaven: our forever home
weeks.nextUp: Week 20 · Palm Sunday: Jesus enters Jerusalem
weeks.bigIdea: Heaven is our forever home: Jesus is preparing a place for us, God will dwell with his people, and he will wipe every tear. We wait for the King and say, “Come, Lord Jesus.”
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 19 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read John 14:1–6 out loud, then Revelation 21:1–7, then Revelation 22:1–5 and 22:20.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Age parts
howSteps.detail: Use Enoch, Elijah, and Jordyn tabs. Keep the Parent key open for yourself.

howSteps.title: Pray
howSteps.detail: Close with the short family prayer on the Prayer tab.

readings.text: 1 “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. 2 My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? 3 And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am. 4 You know the way to the place where I am going.” 5 Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going, so how can we know the way?” 6 Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

1 Then I saw “a new heaven and a new earth,” for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea. 2 I saw the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband. 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. 4 ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” 5 He who was seated on the throne said, “I am making everything new!” Then he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.” 6 He said to me: “It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give water without cost from the spring of the water of life. 7 Those who are victorious will inherit all this, and I will be their God and they will be my children.

1 Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb 2 down the middle of the great street of the city. On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. 3 No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him. 4 They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. 5 There will be no more night. They will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God will give them light. And they will reign for ever and ever. 20 He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

story: Last week we learned to love everyone made in God’s image. This week we look ahead to our forever home. Heaven is not a vague wish. It is the place Jesus is preparing, where God will dwell with his people.

Jesus said to his disciples, “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am.” Thomas did not know the way. Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”

John was later shown a new heaven and a new earth, and the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down from God, prepared as a bride. A loud voice said, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God.” He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. The one on the throne said, “I am making everything new!”

There is a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.” “There will be no more night.” And the last word we hear is a promise and a prayer: “Yes, I am coming soon.” “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”

So this is our hope, and it points us to next week. Palm Sunday is coming. We will watch the King enter Jerusalem — the same Jesus who is preparing a place, who is the way to the Father, and who says, “I am coming soon.” Heaven is our forever home because that King is coming.
weeks.enochLine: Jesus is making a home for us. We will be with him forever!
enochActivities: Activity: A place prepared. Help a grown-up set out a special chair or pillow and say, “Jesus is making a place for us!”
Activity: Come, Lord Jesus. Open your hands and say, “Come, Lord Jesus!”
elijahQuestions: In John 14:2, where is Jesus going, and what is he going to do there?
In John 14:6, what does Jesus say he is?
In Revelation 21:4, what will God wipe from our eyes, and what will there be no more of?
In Revelation 22:20, what does Jesus promise, and what do we say back?
jordynQuestions: Jesus says, “I am going there to prepare a place for you,” and also, “I will come back and take you to be with me” (John 14:2–3). What is heaven, if it is more than a pretty place we go by ourselves?
Revelation 21:3 says God’s dwelling place is now among the people. How does that help you understand why “no more death or mourning or crying or pain” is good news (Revelation 21:4)?
Next week is Palm Sunday, when the King enters Jerusalem. How do John 14:3, “I will come back,” and Revelation 22:20, “Come, Lord Jesus,” get you ready to watch him ride in?
weeks.jordynApplication: Heaven is our forever home because Jesus is the way, and he is preparing a place (John 14:2–6). This week, set your heart on things above (Colossians 3:1–2), and practice the prayer “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20) as you get ready for Palm Sunday.
elijahAnswers: To his Father’s house, to prepare a place for us (John 14:2). “My Father’s house has many rooms,” and “I am going there to prepare a place for you.”
“I am the way and the truth and the life.” “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).
He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain (Revelation 21:4).
Jesus says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” We say, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20).
jordynAnswers: Heaven is being with Jesus, in the Father’s house, in the place he prepares (John 14:2–3). The gift is not only rooms. It is that he comes back and takes us to be with him.

The deepest good of heaven is that God himself will be with his people (Revelation 21:3). When he dwells with them, he wipes every tear, and death, mourning, crying, and pain are gone (Revelation 21:4). The comfort is his presence, not a vague “better place.”

The King who will enter Jerusalem next week is the same Jesus who promises to come back and take us home (John 14:3). Saying “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20) is how we welcome that King — not only one Sunday, but until he comes.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she practiced setting her heart on things above, and whether she prayed “Come, Lord Jesus” as Palm Sunday drew near. If it is fitting, share one way you hoped in the forever home this week too, and pray together for the week ahead.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus has gone to prepare a place for us, and that he is the way to you. Thank you that you will dwell with your people, wipe every tear, and make everything new. Teach us to set our hearts on things above, and give us this prayer: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. In his name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Jesus is going to prepare a place for us, and he will come back and take us to be with him.
dailies.verse: My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you?
dailies.enoch: Help a grown-up make a little “room” with a blanket or pillow and say, “Jesus is making a place for us!”
dailies.elijah: In John 14:1, what does Jesus tell his disciples not to let happen to their hearts?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me.”
dailies.jordyn: Jesus promises both to go and prepare a place, and to come back and take you to be with him (John 14:2–3). Why is “being with him” the center of the promise, not only the rooms?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The rooms matter because they are in the Father’s house, and because Jesus takes us to be where he is (John 14:2–3). Heaven is home because we are with him.
dailies.action: When you feel troubled today, say John 14:1 out loud: “Do not let your hearts be troubled,” and tell a grown-up what you are trusting Jesus with.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, thank you that you are preparing a place for us, and that you will come back and take us to be with you. Help us trust you today. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus tells his disciples not to let their hearts be troubled. His Father’s house has many rooms, and he is going to prepare a place for them. He will come back and take them to be with him. Thomas does not know the way. Jesus says, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.”
dailies.enochActivity: Point down the hallway or toward a door and say, “Jesus is the way home!”
dailies.elijah2: In John 14:6, can anyone come to the Father except through Jesus?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: No. “No one comes to the Father except through me.” He is the way and the truth and the life.
dailies.jordyn2: How does “I am the way” keep heaven from becoming a place we try to reach by being good enough, or by finding our own path?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The way is a Person. Jesus himself is the way to the Father (John 14:6). We do not invent a road to the Father’s house. We trust the one who is going there to prepare a place, and who will come back for us.
dailies.passageText: 1 “Do not let your hearts be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me. 2 My Father’s house has many rooms; if that were not so, would I have told you that I am going there to prepare a place for you? 3 And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am. 4 You know the way to the place where I am going.” 5 Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going, so how can we know the way?” 6 Jesus answered, “I am the way and the truth and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Our citizenship is in heaven, and we wait for the Savior from there.
dailies.verse: But our citizenship is in heaven. And we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ,
dailies.enoch: Put a hand over your heart and say, “My home is with Jesus!”
dailies.elijah: In Philippians 3:20, where is our citizenship?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “But our citizenship is in heaven.” We “eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ.”
dailies.jordyn: If your citizenship is in heaven, how should that change what you are most eager for — not only what you own or win today?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We “eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). Eagerness for him is the mark of a citizen of heaven, more than eagerness for things that stay here.
dailies.action: Play a simple “where is your city?” game: a grown-up names something (a toy, a team, a snack, Jesus), and everyone points to themselves if it is only here, or opens their hands if it belongs to our forever home.
dailies.prayer: Lord Jesus, our citizenship is in heaven. Teach us to wait for you with eager hearts. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Paul says our citizenship is in heaven. We eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ. He will transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body. Our true city is not finally this one. We wait for him.
dailies.enochActivity: March in a little “waiting line” to a chair, sit, and say, “We wait for Jesus!”
dailies.elijah2: In Philippians 3:21, what will Jesus do to our lowly bodies?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He “will transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body,” by the power that enables him to bring everything under his control.
dailies.jordyn2: How does waiting for a Savior “from there” get your heart ready for Palm Sunday, when we watch the King enter Jerusalem?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The King we await is the Lord Jesus Christ (Philippians 3:20). Palm Sunday is a picture of welcoming that King. We practice now the eagerness we will bring to his coming.
dailies.passageText: 20 But our citizenship is in heaven. And we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, 21 who, by the power that enables him to bring everything under his control, will transform our lowly bodies so that they will be like his glorious body.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: God will dwell with his people. He will wipe every tear, and he is making everything new.
dailies.verse: ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.”
dailies.enoch: Gently wipe a pretend tear from a family member’s cheek and say, “God will wipe every tear.”
dailies.elijah: In Revelation 21:3, where will God’s dwelling place be?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Among the people.” “he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God.”
dailies.jordyn: The loud voice does not first list streets or treasures. It says, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people” (Revelation 21:3). Why is that the headline of the new heaven and new earth?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The forever home is God with his people (Revelation 21:3). Tears, death, mourning, crying, and pain end because he is there and is making everything new (Revelation 21:4–5).
dailies.action: Comfort someone who is sad today in a small, concrete way, and tell them God will wipe every tear.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you will dwell with your people and wipe every tear. Help us believe you are making everything new. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: John saw a new heaven and a new earth, and the Holy City coming down from God. A loud voice said that God’s dwelling place is now among the people. He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. The one on the throne said, “I am making everything new!” These words are trustworthy and true.
dailies.enochActivity: Draw a simple picture of a happy city and a smile, and say, “God will be with us.”
dailies.elijah2: In Revelation 21:5, what did the one seated on the throne say, and what did he tell John to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “I am making everything new!” Then he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.”
dailies.jordyn2: Why does it matter that these words are “trustworthy and true,” not only beautiful to imagine?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The one on the throne tells John to write them down because they can be trusted (Revelation 21:5). Our hope is not a daydream. It is the word of the God who will dwell with his people and make everything new.
dailies.passageText: 1 Then I saw “a new heaven and a new earth,” for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away, and there was no longer any sea. 2 I saw the Holy City, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride beautifully dressed for her husband. 3 And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying, “Look! God’s dwelling place is now among the people, and he will dwell with them. They will be his people, and God himself will be with them and be their God. 4 ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” 5 He who was seated on the throne said, “I am making everything new!” Then he said, “Write this down, for these words are trustworthy and true.” 6 He said to me: “It is done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the Beginning and the End. To the thirsty I will give water without cost from the spring of the water of life. 7 Those who are victorious will inherit all this, and I will be their God and they will be my children.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: You have been raised with Christ. Set your heart and mind on things above, where Christ is.
dailies.verse: Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.
dailies.enoch: Look up, then look at a grown-up, and say, “I can think about Jesus!”
dailies.elijah: In Colossians 3:1, where should we set our hearts, and why?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “set your hearts on things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God,” because “you have been raised with Christ.”
dailies.jordyn: Setting your mind on things above is not pretending earth does not matter. What is the difference between hoping in heaven and ignoring the people in front of you?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We set our minds on things above because we have been raised with Christ, who is there (Colossians 3:1–2). That hope should make us more faithful here, not less — loving people made in God’s image while we wait for our forever home.
dailies.action: Challenge: choose one earthly thing you often cling to (a screen, a score, a snack, a worry). Put it down for a set time today, and use that time to pray, serve, or read a little of this week’s passage.
dailies.prayer: Father, we have been raised with Christ. Help us set our hearts and minds on things above, where he is. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Since we have been raised with Christ, we set our hearts on things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. We set our minds on things above, not on earthly things. This is how citizens of heaven live now, while we wait for him to appear.
dailies.enochActivity: Put one toy in a basket for a little while and say, “Jesus first!”
dailies.elijah2: In Colossians 3:2, what should we set our minds on, and what should we not set them on?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things.”
dailies.jordyn2: Colossians 3:4 says that when Christ, who is your life, appears, you also will appear with him in glory. How does that make “things above” more than a hobby?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Christ himself is your life, and you will appear with him in glory (Colossians 3:4). Setting your mind on things above is setting your mind on him — the one who will appear, and the one we will welcome on Palm Sunday as King.
dailies.passageText: 1 Since, then, you have been raised with Christ, set your hearts on things above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. 2 Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. 3 For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God. 4 When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: They will see his face. Jesus says, “I am coming soon.” We pray, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”
dailies.verse: He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands and pray, “Come, Lord Jesus.”
dailies.elijah: In Revelation 22:4, what will they see?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads.”
dailies.jordyn: The river of the water of life flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb, and “they will see his face” (Revelation 22:1, 4). How is seeing his face the heart of the forever home?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The home is not only a beautiful city. It is God and the Lamb, and his people seeing his face (Revelation 22:1–4). The joy of heaven is nearness to him.
dailies.action: Pray “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus” at bedtime tonight, and tell a grown-up one thing you are glad Jesus is coming to make new.
dailies.prayer: Lord Jesus, thank you that we will see your face, and that there will be no more night. You say, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
dailies.teach: The angel showed John the river of the water of life, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb. They will see his face. There will be no more night, for the Lord God will give them light. And Jesus says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” The church’s prayer is, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”
dailies.enochActivity: With a grown-up, look at a light in the room, then pray, “Thank you, God, that there will be no more night.”
dailies.elijah2: In Revelation 22:20, what does the one who testifies say, and what is the answering prayer?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” The answering prayer is, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.”
dailies.jordyn2: Tomorrow we recap this week, and Sunday is Palm Sunday. Why is “Come, Lord Jesus” the right prayer to carry from a heaven week into a week when the King enters Jerusalem?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The King who enters Jerusalem is the same Lord who promises, “I am coming soon” (Revelation 22:20). Palm Sunday is a welcome. This prayer is how we welcome him — then, now, and when he comes again.
dailies.passageText: 1 Then the angel showed me the river of the water of life, as clear as crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb 2 down the middle of the great street of the city. On each side of the river stood the tree of life, bearing twelve crops of fruit, yielding its fruit every month. And the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations. 3 No longer will there be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in the city, and his servants will serve him. 4 They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. 5 There will be no more night. They will not need the light of a lamp or the light of the sun, for the Lord God will give them light. And they will reign for ever and ever. 20 He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Jesus is preparing a place. God will wipe every tear. We say, “Come, Lord Jesus,” and get ready to welcome the King.
dailies.verse: He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Say this week’s line out loud: “Jesus is making a home for us. We will be with him forever!”
dailies.elijah: Can you tell, in your own words, what Jesus is doing in John 14, and what God will do in Revelation 21:4?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Jesus is preparing a place in his Father’s house, and he will come back and take us to be with him (John 14:2–3). God will wipe every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain (Revelation 21:4).
dailies.jordyn: How do John 14:3, Revelation 21:4, and Revelation 22:20 fit together as one week — and how do they lead you into Palm Sunday tomorrow?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus is preparing a place and will come back (John 14:3). God will dwell with his people and wipe every tear (Revelation 21:3–4). We answer, “Come, Lord Jesus” (Revelation 22:20). Tomorrow we watch that same King enter Jerusalem. The forever home and the welcome of the King belong together.
dailies.action: Look back on the week: where did you set your mind on things above, and where did your heart get troubled? Tell a grown-up, and pray “Come, Lord Jesus” as you get ready for Palm Sunday.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for our forever home. Jesus is the way, you will wipe every tear, and you are making everything new. As we go toward Palm Sunday, we pray: Amen. Come, Lord Jesus. In his name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that heaven is our forever home. Jesus is preparing a place, and he is the way to the Father. God will dwell with his people and wipe every tear. We wait with the prayer, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.” Next we watch the King enter Jerusalem — the same Jesus who is coming to take us home.
dailies.enochActivity: Make a simple “welcome” sign with a grown-up that says, “Come, Lord Jesus,” and save it for tomorrow.
dailies.elijah2: In John 14:3, what two things does Jesus say he will do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He will go and prepare a place for us, and he will come back and take us to be with him, so that we also may be where he is.
dailies.jordyn2: What is one concrete way you can welcome the King this Palm Sunday week — in your house, at church, or in how you wait?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: a glad welcome at church, the prayer “Come, Lord Jesus,” setting your mind on things above, or serving someone as a citizen of heaven. The welcome is not only a palm branch. It is a heart ready for the King who is the way home.
dailies.passageText: And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come back and take you to be with me that you also may be where I am. ‘He will wipe every tear from their eyes. There will be no more death’ or mourning or crying or pain, for the old order of things has passed away.” 20 He who testifies to these things says, “Yes, I am coming soon.” Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

weeks.title: Palm Sunday: Jesus enters Jerusalem
weeks.selectLabel: Week 20 · Palm Sunday: Jesus enters Jerusalem
weeks.nextUp: Week 21 · Easter: Jesus is risen
weeks.bigIdea: Jesus is the promised King. He enters Jerusalem gentle and riding on a donkey, and the crowds shout, “Hosanna!” — “LORD, save us!” We welcome him, and next week we see how he saves: he is risen.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 20 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Zechariah 9:9 out loud, then Matthew 21:1–11, then John 12:12–19.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

readings.text: 9 Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples, 2 saying to them, “Go to the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt by her. Untie them and bring them to me. 3 If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.” 4 This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: 5 “Say to Daughter Zion, ‘See, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’” 6 The disciples went and did as Jesus had instructed them. 7 They brought the donkey and the colt and placed their cloaks on them for Jesus to sit on. 8 A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. 9 The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” 10 When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” 11 The crowds answered, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”

12 The next day the great crowd that had come for the festival heard that Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem. 13 They took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!” 14 Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, as it is written: 15 “Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.” 16 At first his disciples did not understand all this. Only after Jesus was glorified did they realize that these things had been written about him and that these things had been done to him. 17 Now the crowd that was with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to spread the word. 18 Many people, because they had heard that he had performed this sign, went out to meet him. 19 So the Pharisees said to one another, “See, this is getting us nowhere. Look how the whole world has gone after him!”

story: Last week we looked ahead to our forever home, and we prayed, “Come, Lord Jesus.” This week the King comes into Jerusalem. Long before, the Lord had promised, “Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”

As Jesus came near the city, he sent two disciples to find a donkey and a colt. This happened to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: “Say to Daughter Zion, ‘See, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’” The disciples brought the donkey, laid their cloaks on it, and Jesus sat on them. A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road.

The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” The crowds answered, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”

John tells us they took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!” This is what “Hosanna” means: “LORD, save us!” The King they welcome is coming to save.
So we wave and we shout with them. And we look toward next week. This King does not turn aside. He enters Jerusalem to save his people. Next Sunday we will see how he saves: Jesus is risen.
weeks.enochLine: Jesus is the King! We shout, Hosanna!
enochActivities: Activity: A road for the King. Help a grown-up lay a coat or towel on the floor and say, “Hosanna! Jesus is the King!”
Activity: Palm branches. Wave a green leaf, a paper branch, or your hands and shout, “Hosanna!”
elijahQuestions: In Zechariah 9:9, how does the promised king come to Daughter Zion?
In Matthew 21:9, what did the crowds shout as Jesus rode into Jerusalem?
In John 12:13, what did the people take in their hands as they went out to meet Jesus?
What does “Hosanna” mean, from Psalm 118:25?
jordynQuestions: Zechariah 9:9 and Matthew 21:5 both show a king on a donkey, not a war horse. What kind of King is Jesus, if he comes “lowly” and “gentle”?
The crowds shout, “Hosanna!” which means, “LORD, save us!” (Psalm 118:25). How does that cry get you ready for Easter next week?
In Luke 19:40 Jesus says, “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.” What does it mean to welcome this King with more than a shout one Sunday?
weeks.jordynApplication: Jesus is the promised King who enters Jerusalem to save (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5, 9). This week, practice the shout “Hosanna” — “LORD, save us!” — and get ready for Easter, when we see that this King is risen.
elijahAnswers: “lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9).
“Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” (Matthew 21:9).
Palm branches (John 12:13).
“LORD, save us!” (Psalm 118:25).
jordynAnswers: He is righteous and victorious, yet he comes lowly and gentle, riding on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5). He is a saving King, not a king who comes to crush his people.
“Hosanna” is a prayer for the King to save (Psalm 118:25). Next week we see how he saves: Jesus is risen. The welcome of Palm Sunday and the joy of Easter belong together.
The stones would cry out if the people were silent (Luke 19:40). Welcoming the King means we keep praising him, and we follow him into the week when he saves — toward the empty tomb next Sunday.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she practiced the prayer “Hosanna” — “LORD, save us!” — and whether she is looking toward Easter. If it is fitting, share one way you welcomed the King this week too, and pray together for the week ahead.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus is the promised King, who comes gentle and riding on a donkey. We shout with the crowds, “Hosanna!” — “LORD, save us!” Teach us to welcome him this week, and get our hearts ready for Easter, when we see that he is risen. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Jesus enters Jerusalem as the promised King, and the crowds shout, “Hosanna to the Son of David!”
dailies.verse: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
dailies.enoch: Lay a coat or towel on the floor like a road and say, “Hosanna! Jesus is the King!”
dailies.elijah: In Matthew 21:5, how does the king come to Daughter Zion?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “See, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”
dailies.jordyn: The whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” (Matthew 21:10). How would you answer, using what the crowds shouted in Matthew 21:9?
dailies.jordynAnswer: This is Jesus, the Son of David, the King who comes in the name of the Lord (Matthew 21:9–11). “Hosanna” is how we welcome him.
dailies.action: Tell someone today that Jesus is the King, and say “Hosanna” as a real prayer: “LORD, save us.”
dailies.prayer: Jesus, you are the King who comes gentle and riding on a donkey. We welcome you with the crowds: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: As Jesus came near Jerusalem, he sent two disciples for a donkey and a colt, to fulfill the prophet’s word: the king comes gentle and riding on a donkey. The crowd spread cloaks and branches on the road. They shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” The whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?”
dailies.enochActivity: Wave your hands or a green leaf and shout, “Hosanna!”
dailies.elijah2: In Matthew 21:9, what three shouts did the crowds cry?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
dailies.jordyn2: Why does it matter that Jesus comes “gentle and riding on a donkey,” not on a war horse?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: This is the King God promised (Matthew 21:4–5). He is victorious, but he comes gently, to save. Palm Sunday shows us what kind of King he is before we watch, next week, how he saves.
dailies.passageText: 1 As they approached Jerusalem and came to Bethphage on the Mount of Olives, Jesus sent two disciples, 2 saying to them, “Go to the village ahead of you, and at once you will find a donkey tied there, with her colt by her. Untie them and bring them to me. 3 If anyone says anything to you, say that the Lord needs them, and he will send them right away.” 4 This took place to fulfill what was spoken through the prophet: 5 “Say to Daughter Zion, ‘See, your king comes to you, gentle and riding on a donkey, and on a colt, the foal of a donkey.’” 6 The disciples went and did as Jesus had instructed them. 7 They brought the donkey and the colt and placed their cloaks on them for Jesus to sit on. 8 A very large crowd spread their cloaks on the road, while others cut branches from the trees and spread them on the road. 9 The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” 10 When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred and asked, “Who is this?” 11 The crowds answered, “This is Jesus, the prophet from Nazareth in Galilee.”

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: The prophet promised a king who comes lowly, riding on a donkey. Jesus is that King.
dailies.verse: Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.
dailies.enoch: Trot like a donkey (gently!) and then sit down and say, “The King comes on a donkey!”
dailies.elijah: In Zechariah 9:9, what is Daughter Zion told to do, and how does her king come?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem!” The king comes “righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”
dailies.jordyn: Zechariah 9:9 calls the king both “victorious” and “lowly.” How can both be true in Jesus as he rides into Jerusalem?
dailies.jordynAnswer: He is the true King, righteous and victorious, yet he comes lowly, on a donkey, just as God promised (Zechariah 9:9). His victory will look like saving his people, which we will see at Easter.
dailies.action: Play a “which King?” game: one person pretends to be a proud king, another comes lowly on a “donkey.” Talk about which picture matches Zechariah 9:9.
dailies.prayer: Lord, thank you that you promised a king who comes lowly, riding on a donkey. Thank you that Jesus is that King. Help us rejoice and shout. In his name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Long before Palm Sunday, the Lord told Daughter Zion to rejoice and shout. Her king would come righteous and victorious, yet lowly, riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. When Jesus sent for the donkey and rode into Jerusalem, he was keeping that promise.
dailies.enochActivity: Shout, “Rejoice! The King is coming!” and give a big smile.
dailies.elijah2: In Zechariah 9:9, what animal does the king ride?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: A donkey — “on a colt, the foal of a donkey.”
dailies.jordyn2: Why is it good news that this King is “lowly,” not only “victorious”?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: A lowly King can be approached. He comes to save, not to trample his people (Zechariah 9:9). That is why we can shout “Hosanna” and mean it.
dailies.passageText: 9 Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: The people take palm branches and go out to meet Jesus, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!”
dailies.verse: They took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!”
dailies.enoch: Wave a green leaf or a paper palm and say, “Blessed is the king!”
dailies.elijah: In John 12:13, what three shouts did the people cry as they met Jesus with palm branches?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!”
dailies.jordyn: John 12:15 says, “Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.” How does “Do not be afraid” belong with welcoming the King?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The King who comes is for his people, not against them (John 12:15). We do not have to be afraid to welcome him. He comes to save.
dailies.action: Make or color a simple palm branch, and write “Hosanna” on it. Put it where you will see it this week.
dailies.prayer: Jesus, we take up the shout of the crowd: “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!” In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The great crowd that had come for the festival heard that Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem. They took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!” This was to fulfill the word, “Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.”
dailies.enochActivity: Hold your “palm” high and say, “Do not be afraid! The King is coming!”
dailies.elijah2: In John 12:15, what is Daughter Zion told not to do, and what should she see?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.”
dailies.jordyn2: The Pharisees said, “Look how the whole world has gone after him!” (John 12:19). What do their words, even if meant as a complaint, tell you about this King?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The welcome of Jesus cannot be kept small (John 12:19). He is the King of Israel, and the world is being drawn to him. We join that welcome.
dailies.passageText: 12 The next day the great crowd that had come for the festival heard that Jesus was on his way to Jerusalem. 13 They took palm branches and went out to meet him, shouting, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Blessed is the king of Israel!” 14 Jesus found a young donkey and sat on it, as it is written: 15 “Do not be afraid, Daughter Zion; see, your king is coming, seated on a donkey’s colt.” 16 At first his disciples did not understand all this. Only after Jesus was glorified did they realize that these things had been written about him and that these things had been done to him. 17 Now the crowd that was with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead continued to spread the word. 18 Many people, because they had heard that he had performed this sign, went out to meet him. 19 So the Pharisees said to one another, “See, this is getting us nowhere. Look how the whole world has gone after him!”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: “Hosanna” means “LORD, save us!” Even children praise the King.
dailies.verse: LORD, save us! LORD, grant us success! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you.
dailies.enoch: Say slowly, “LORD, save us!” Then shout, “Hosanna!”
dailies.elijah: In Psalm 118:25–26, what does the first shout ask the LORD to do, and who is blessed?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “LORD, save us! LORD, grant us success!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD.”
dailies.jordyn: The children in the temple shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matthew 21:15). Why is it fitting that children praise this King, and how does Psalm 118 help you understand their shout?
dailies.jordynAnswer: “Hosanna” is Psalm 118:25: “LORD, save us!” The children are not only being noisy. They are praying the Bible’s welcome of the King. Jesus is pleased with their praise (Matthew 21:16).
dailies.action: Teach someone younger (or practice yourself) that “Hosanna” means “LORD, save us!” Say it as a prayer, not only as a cheer.
dailies.prayer: LORD, save us! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. We welcome Jesus as King, and we ask you to save. In his name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The shout “Hosanna” comes from Psalm 118: “LORD, save us! LORD, grant us success! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you.” When the crowds and the children cried “Hosanna,” they were asking the King to save. In the temple, children shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David,” and Jesus welcomed their praise.
dailies.enochActivity: Clap and say, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD!”
dailies.elijah2: In Matthew 21:15, what did the children shout in the temple?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “Hosanna to the Son of David.”
dailies.jordyn2: How can “Hosanna” be both a cheer and a prayer this week, as we walk toward Easter?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We gladly welcome the King, and we ask him to save (Psalm 118:25–26). Easter is the answer to that prayer: the King who entered the city has died and is risen.
dailies.passageText: 25 LORD, save us! LORD, grant us success! 26 Blessed is he who comes in the name of the LORD. From the house of the LORD we bless you.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: If the people keep quiet, the stones will cry out. We will not keep quiet. We welcome the King.
dailies.verse: “I tell you,” he replied, “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.”
dailies.enoch: Pick up a small stone, hold it, and say, “We will praise Jesus!” Then set it down.
dailies.elijah: In Luke 19:38, what did the crowd of disciples shout as Jesus came down the Mount of Olives?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!”
dailies.jordyn: Some of the Pharisees wanted Jesus to rebuke his disciples (Luke 19:39). Why does Jesus answer, “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out”?
dailies.jordynAnswer: This King must be praised (Luke 19:40). If people will not welcome him, creation itself would cry out. We do not need to be silent. We get to praise him.
dailies.action: Pray Luke 19:38 out loud as a family: “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord!”
dailies.prayer: Jesus, we will not keep quiet. Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven and glory in the highest! In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Jesus went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. As he came down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of disciples began to praise God with loud voices for all the miracles they had seen. They shouted, “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” Some Pharisees told Jesus to rebuke his disciples. He replied, “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.”
dailies.enochActivity: Thank you, God, that Jesus is the King. We will not keep quiet!
dailies.elijah2: In Luke 19:40, what did Jesus say would happen if the people kept quiet?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.”
dailies.jordyn2: What is one way you can refuse to “keep quiet” about this King this week, without being showy — a word, a song, a kindness done in his name?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: saying “Hosanna” as a prayer, telling someone Jesus is the King, singing, or serving someone in his name. The point is a real welcome, not a silent heart (Luke 19:40).
dailies.passageText: 28 After Jesus had said this, he went on ahead, going up to Jerusalem. 29 As he approached Bethphage and Bethany at the hill called the Mount of Olives, he sent two of his disciples, saying to them, 30 “Go to the village ahead of you, and as you enter it, you will find a colt tied there, which no one has ever ridden. Untie it and bring it here. 31 If anyone asks you, ‘Why are you untying it?’ say, ‘The Lord needs it.’” 32 Those who were sent ahead went and found it just as he had told them. 33 As they were untying the colt, its owners asked them, “Why are you untying the colt?” 34 They replied, “The Lord needs it.” 35 They brought it to Jesus, threw their cloaks on the colt and put Jesus on it. 36 As he went along, people spread their cloaks on the road. 37 When he came near the place where the road goes down the Mount of Olives, the whole crowd of disciples began joyfully to praise God in loud voices for all the miracles they had seen: 38 “Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Peace in heaven and glory in the highest!” 39 Some of the Pharisees in the crowd said to Jesus, “Teacher, rebuke your disciples!” 40 “I tell you,” he replied, “if they keep quiet, the stones will cry out.”

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: The promised King has come. We shout, “Hosanna!” — “LORD, save us!” — and get ready for Easter.
dailies.verse: “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
dailies.enoch: Wave and shout one more time: “Hosanna! Jesus is the King!” Then say, “Next we celebrate: Jesus is risen!”
dailies.elijah: Can you tell, in your own words, how Jesus entered Jerusalem, and what the people shouted?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He came riding on a donkey, just as God promised (Zechariah 9:9; Matthew 21:5). The people spread cloaks and branches, even palm branches, and shouted, “Hosanna!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!”
dailies.jordyn: How do Zechariah 9:9, “Hosanna” in Matthew 21:9, and Easter next Sunday fit together as one story?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God promised a lowly, victorious King (Zechariah 9:9). The crowds welcome him with “Hosanna” — “LORD, save us!” (Matthew 21:9; Psalm 118:25). Next Sunday we see how he saves: Jesus is risen. The welcome and the rescue belong together.
dailies.action: Before bed, thank Jesus that he is the King who came to save, and ask him to get your heart ready for Easter tomorrow.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus is the promised King. We have shouted, “Hosanna!” — “LORD, save us!” As we go toward Easter, we praise you that this King saves, and that he is risen. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that Jesus is the promised King. He entered Jerusalem gentle and lowly, riding on a donkey. The people took palm branches and shouted, “Hosanna!” — “LORD, save us!” If they had kept quiet, the stones would have cried out. Next we watch how this King saves: Easter is coming, and Jesus is risen.
dailies.enochActivity: Give a grown-up a hug and say, “Jesus is the King, and he saves!”
dailies.elijah2: What does “Hosanna” mean, and why does that matter as we get ready for Easter?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: It means “LORD, save us!” (Psalm 118:25). Easter is when we see that the King who entered the city has saved — he is risen.
dailies.jordyn2: What is one way you will welcome the King tomorrow, on Easter, that grows out of this week’s “Hosanna”?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Answers will vary: a glad welcome at church, the prayer “LORD, save us,” telling someone Jesus is risen, or praising him instead of keeping quiet. Palm Sunday’s shout and Easter’s joy are one welcome of the same King.
dailies.passageText: Rejoice greatly, Daughter Zion! Shout, Daughter Jerusalem! See, your king comes to you, righteous and victorious, lowly and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey. The crowds that went ahead of him and those that followed shouted, “Hosanna to the Son of David!” “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord!” “Hosanna in the highest heaven!” LORD, save us! LORD, grant us success!

weeks.bigIdea: Jesus died, and the tomb is empty: “He is not here; he has risen, just as he said.” He meets his friends, says “Peace be with you,” and sends them to tell the good news.
weeks.scheduleNote: This is the Week 21 family lesson. The short daily bites are Days 2–7.

howSteps.title: Read together
howSteps.detail: Open the Read tab and read Matthew 28:1–10 out loud, then John 20:11–18, then Luke 24:36–49.

howSteps.title: Talk it through
howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.

howSteps.title: Pray
