readings.text: 8 Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. 9 Opposition arose, however, from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called)—Jews of Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia—who began to argue with Stephen. 10 But they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. 11 Then they secretly persuaded some men to say, “We have heard Stephen speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God.” 12 So they stirred up the people and the elders and the teachers of the law. They seized Stephen and brought him before the Sanhedrin. 13 They produced false witnesses, who testified, “This fellow never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. 14 For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down to us.” 15 All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

54 When the members of the Sanhedrin heard this, they were furious and gnashed their teeth at him. 55 But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. 56 “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” 57 At this they covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him, 58 dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile, the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

story: Last week we saw the first church pray, learn, and share so no one was in need. This week we see that the same church also had people who stayed faithful to Jesus when it was hard. Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life.

Stephen was a man full of God’s grace and power, and he performed great wonders and signs among the people. Some men began to argue with him, but they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. So they secretly stirred up people and produced false witnesses, who said he never stopped speaking against the holy place and the law. They seized Stephen and brought him before the Sanhedrin. All who were sitting there looked intently at him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

Stephen told them the long story of how God had been faithful to his people, and he told them the truth: they had resisted the Holy Spirit, and they had betrayed and murdered the Righteous One, Jesus. When they heard this, they were furious. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

They covered their ears, rushed at him, dragged him out of the city, and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. This is a hard and sad part of the story, and we tell it with care, not as a game. While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep. That is the Bible’s gentle way of saying he died, and the Lord Jesus received him.

Stephen was faithful to the end. He told the truth, he saw Jesus, and he even prayed for the people who were hurting him. Next week we will see that God kept sending the good news. God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus.
weeks.enochLine: Stephen told the truth about Jesus, and Jesus was with him!
enochActivities: Activity: Stand tall. Stand up straight, look up, and say: Jesus is with me!
Activity: Kind prayer. Fold your hands and say: Lord Jesus, help me love people, even when it is hard.
elijahQuestions: In Acts 6:8, what was Stephen full of, and what did he do among the people?
In Acts 6:10, why could the men who argued with Stephen not stand up against him?
In Acts 7:55–56, what did Stephen see when he looked up to heaven?
In Acts 7:59–60, what two prayers did Stephen pray while they were stoning him?
elijahAnswers: He was full of God’s grace and power, and he performed great wonders and signs among the people (Acts 6:8).
They could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke (Acts 6:10).
He saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. He said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” (Acts 7:55–56).
“Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” And, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” (Acts 7:59–60).
jordynQuestions: The men could not answer Stephen’s wisdom, so they used false witnesses (Acts 6:10–13). What does that show about telling the truth when people will not listen fairly?
Stephen saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55–56), and then he prayed for the people who were hurting him (Acts 7:59–60). How do those two things belong together?

This week Stephen is faithful even when it costs him his life. Next week God will send Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. What does that tell you about God’s work after a very hard day?
jordynAnswers: Faithfulness is not the same as winning an argument. Stephen kept telling the truth about Jesus even when people made up lies. The Spirit gave him wisdom, and he did not have to become false in order to be heard.

He can see that Jesus is alive and in glory, so he can trust Jesus with his life and even with his enemies. “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit” is trust. “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” is mercy, like Jesus’ own prayer.

The story of Jesus does not stop when one of his people dies. God is still sending the good news. Next week we will see Philip sent to help a man understand it. Stephen was faithful, and God is still at work.
weeks.jordynApplication: Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life (Acts 6:8–15; 7:54–60). This week, tell the truth about Jesus in one hard moment, and ask the Lord to help you forgive. Next week we will see that God kept sending the good news through Philip.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether there was a moment when it was hard to tell the truth about Jesus, or hard to forgive. If it is fitting, thank God together that Jesus stood for Stephen, and that we can ask him for the same faithfulness and mercy.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Stephen was full of your Spirit and told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life. Thank you that he saw Jesus standing in heaven, and that he prayed for the people who hurt him. Make us faithful too, and keep sending your good news. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Stephen is full of God’s grace and power, and the Spirit gives him wisdom to speak.
dailies.verse: Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.
dailies.enoch: Stand tall and say: God can make me brave to tell the truth!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 6:8–10, what was Stephen full of, and what could the men who argued with him not stand up against?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He was full of God’s grace and power. They could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke.
dailies.jordyn: In Acts 6:13, they produced false witnesses. What does that tell you about why some people opposed Stephen?
dailies.jordynAnswer: They could not beat the wisdom the Spirit gave him, so they told lies about him. Opposition to the truth is not always honest. Stephen still stands there with a face like the face of an angel (Acts 6:15).
dailies.action: Read Acts 6:8–15 together, then tell someone: Stephen was full of God’s grace and power, and the Spirit gave him wisdom.
dailies.prayer: Father, fill us with your grace and power, and give us the wisdom of your Spirit, so we can tell the truth about Jesus with a faithful heart. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Stephen was full of God’s grace and power, and he performed great wonders and signs among the people. Some argued with him, but they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. They secretly stirred up people, produced false witnesses, and brought Stephen before the Sanhedrin. All who were sitting there looked intently at him, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look at your face, then smile a calm smile, and say: The Spirit can make us brave and kind.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 6:15, what did the Sanhedrin see when they looked at Stephen?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
dailies.jordyn2: Why does it matter that Luke tells us about Stephen’s face before he tells us what happened next?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The room is already angry, and Stephen is already at peace. His faithfulness is not only in his words. The Spirit’s work can be seen even before the hardest moment comes.
dailies.passageText: 8 Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. 9 Opposition arose, however, from members of the Synagogue of the Freedmen (as it was called)—Jews of Cyrene and Alexandria as well as the provinces of Cilicia and Asia—who began to argue with Stephen. 10 But they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. 11 Then they secretly persuaded some men to say, “We have heard Stephen speak blasphemous words against Moses and against God.” 12 So they stirred up the people and the elders and the teachers of the law. They seized Stephen and brought him before the Sanhedrin. 13 They produced false witnesses, who testified, “This fellow never stops speaking against this holy place and against the law. 14 For we have heard him say that this Jesus of Nazareth will destroy this place and change the customs Moses handed down to us.” 15 All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Practice standing firm and telling the truth about Jesus, without turning his suffering into a game.
dailies.verse: All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.
dailies.enoch: Stand still, look up, and say: I can be faithful to Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 6:10, who gave Stephen the wisdom to speak?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Spirit gave him wisdom as he spoke.
dailies.jordyn: How should we practice being faithful so that we honor Stephen’s story, and do not pretend the stones or the hurt?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not act out the stoning, and we do not make his death a joke. We practice standing firm, telling the truth about Jesus, and keeping a peaceful face, because the Spirit made Stephen faithful.
dailies.action: Play a stand-firm game: take turns standing tall, looking up, and saying one true sentence about Jesus, such as Jesus is Lord, or Jesus is alive. Cheer for one another’s courage, not for pretend fighting.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Stephen’s face was peaceful because your Spirit was with him. Teach us to stand firm and tell the truth about Jesus, with kindness and courage. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: They could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. And when the Sanhedrin looked at Stephen, they saw that his face was like the face of an angel. Today we practice that kind of faithfulness: standing firm and telling the truth, not playing at anyone being hurt.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up stand with you, look up, and say: Jesus is Lord!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 6:8, what two words describe what Stephen was full of?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: God’s grace and power.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is a peaceful, faithful face a better way to remember Stephen than a game about stones?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The stones are real and sad. What we are meant to copy is his faithfulness, his wisdom from the Spirit, and his peace in Jesus, not the violence that was done to him.
dailies.passageText: 10 But they could not stand up against the wisdom the Spirit gave him as he spoke. 15 All who were sitting in the Sanhedrin looked intently at Stephen, and they saw that his face was like the face of an angel.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Full of the Holy Spirit, Stephen looks up and sees Jesus standing in heaven.
dailies.verse: Look, I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.
dailies.enoch: Look up and say: Jesus is in heaven, and he sees me!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 7:54–55, how did the Sanhedrin feel, and what did Stephen do instead of looking at their anger?
dailies.elijahAnswer: They were furious and gnashed their teeth at him. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
dailies.jordyn: Stephen had just told them the truth about the Righteous One (Acts 7:52). Why does it matter that he sees Jesus standing, not only sitting, at the right hand of God?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus is alive, in glory, and with Stephen in this hardest moment. Stephen is not alone before angry people. The Son of Man is standing, and Stephen can tell the truth because he can see him.
dailies.action: Read Acts 7:54–56 together, then tell someone: Stephen saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus is alive and standing in heaven. When we are afraid, help us look up to him, full of your Spirit, and keep telling the truth. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: When the Sanhedrin heard Stephen’s words, they were furious. But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look up with you and say: I see Jesus is King!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 7:55, what was Stephen full of when he looked up?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The Holy Spirit.
dailies.jordyn2: The room is furious, and Stephen looks up. What does that teach you about where to look when people are against the truth?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He does not win by staring back in anger. He is full of the Holy Spirit, and he looks up to Jesus. Faithfulness looks to the Son of Man, even when the room is loud.
dailies.passageText: 54 When the members of the Sanhedrin heard this, they were furious and gnashed their teeth at him. 55 But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. 56 “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.”

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Be faithful to tell the truth about Jesus, even in a hard moment this week.
dailies.verse: Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Lord Jesus, I belong to you!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 7:59, what did Stephen pray while they were stoning him?
dailies.elijahAnswer: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”
dailies.jordyn: Stephen’s hardest moment is not a child’s game, but his faithfulness still gives you a challenge. What would it look like for you to tell the truth about Jesus in one hard moment this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer: It may be telling the truth when it would be easier to stay quiet, or being kind when someone is unfair, or saying you belong to Jesus. Faithfulness starts in real life, with a heart that trusts Jesus to receive us.
dailies.action: Choose one hard moment this week — at home, at school, or with a friend — and tell the truth about Jesus there, or stay faithful when it would be easier not to.
dailies.prayer: Father, we belong to Jesus. Make us faithful in the real, hard moments of this week, and teach us to trust him with our lives, as Stephen did. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: They covered their ears, rushed at Stephen, dragged him out of the city, and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” We tell this with care. The challenge for us is not to pretend we are being hurt. It is to be faithful to Jesus and to trust him with our lives.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up hold your hands and say: Lord Jesus, we belong to you.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 7:58, where did they take Stephen, and whose feet held the witnesses’ coats?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: They dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. The witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul.
dailies.jordyn2: Luke names Saul here, but he does not yet tell us how Jesus will later change him. Why is it enough, this week, to notice that Stephen stays faithful even then?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The spotlight stays on Jesus and on Stephen’s trust: “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” God can still work in a room this hard, and next week we will see that he keeps sending the good news. We do not have to rush ahead to Saul’s later story to see Stephen’s faithfulness today.
dailies.passageText: 57 At this they covered their ears and, yelling at the top of their voices, they all rushed at him, 58 dragged him out of the city and began to stone him. Meanwhile, the witnesses laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul. 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.”

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Pray like Stephen: trust Jesus with your life, and ask him to forgive.
dailies.verse: Lord, do not hold this sin against them.
dailies.enoch: Fold your hands and say: Lord, help me forgive.
dailies.elijah: In Acts 7:60, what did Stephen cry out, and what happened when he had said this?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.
dailies.jordyn: Stephen prays for the people who are hurting him, after he has already trusted Jesus with his spirit (Acts 7:59–60). How can that shape the way you pray for someone who has been unkind?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We can tell Jesus the truth, ask him to receive us, and then ask him not to hold that person’s sin against them. Forgiveness is not pretending the hurt was nothing. It is asking the Lord to be merciful, as Stephen did.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank Jesus that he received Stephen, and name one person you need help to forgive.
dailies.prayer: Lord Jesus, receive us, and teach us to pray, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Make us faithful and merciful, like Stephen, because we belong to you. In your name, Amen.
dailies.teach: While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep. That is how a faithful man prayed at the end: he trusted Jesus, and he asked for mercy on the people who hurt him.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up pray a short sentence with you: Lord Jesus, help us forgive.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 7:60, what does “he fell asleep” mean in this story?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: It is the Bible’s gentle way of saying Stephen died, and the Lord Jesus received him.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is Stephen’s last prayer a good way for a church to remember him, not only his courage to speak?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He is not only brave. He is merciful. The man who told the truth also prayed for his enemies. Faithfulness to Jesus includes both a true word and a forgiving heart.
dailies.passageText: 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life, and next God will send Philip with the good news.
dailies.verse: Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people.
dailies.enoch: Stand tall, look up, and say: Stephen was faithful, and Jesus is with us!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 6:8 and 7:59–60, what kind of man was Stephen, and how did he finish?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He was full of God’s grace and power, and at the end he prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” and “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Then he fell asleep.
dailies.jordyn: This week Stephen was faithful even when it cost him his life. How does that get your heart ready for next week, when God sends Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The good news does not stop on a hard day. Stephen was faithful, and God is still sending witnesses. Next week we will see Philip sent to help a man understand the good news about Jesus.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life. Then thank God, and look ahead to Philip.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life. Thank you that he saw Jesus standing, and that he prayed for his enemies. Keep sending your good news, and get our hearts ready for the next story. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life. He was full of God’s grace and power, and the Spirit gave him wisdom. He looked up and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. He prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit,” and “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” Next week we will see that God kept sending the good news: God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up open a hand as if sending someone, and say: Next week God will send Philip with the good news!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 7:55–56 and 7:60, what two things did Stephen do at the end?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He looked up and saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God, and he prayed that the Lord would not hold this sin against them.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is faithful to Jesus a fitting last word before a week about Philip and a man who needs help understanding the good news?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Stephen shows us that Jesus’ people tell the truth and trust him to the end. Next week we will see that Jesus still sends help so that someone else can understand that same good news. Faithfulness and going with the message belong to the same Lord.
dailies.passageText: 8 Now Stephen, a man full of God’s grace and power, performed great wonders and signs among the people. 55 But Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked up to heaven and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God. 56 “Look,” he said, “I see heaven open and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God.” 59 While they were stoning him, Stephen prayed, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit.” 60 Then he fell on his knees and cried out, “Lord, do not hold this sin against them.” When he had said this, he fell asleep.

readings.text: 26 Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” 27 So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake (which means “queen of the Ethiopians”). This man had gone to Jerusalem to worship, 28 and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the Book of Isaiah the prophet. 29 The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” 30 Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

32 This is the passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. 33 In his humiliation he was deprived of justice. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth.” 34 The eunuch asked Philip, “Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” 35 Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.

36 As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” 38 And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him. 39 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. 40 Philip, however, appeared at Azotus and traveled about, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

story: Last week Stephen told the truth about Jesus, even when it cost him his life. God did not stop sending the good news. An angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” Philip started out.

On the way he met an important official from Ethiopia, a man in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, which means queen of the Ethiopians. The Bible also calls him a eunuch, a royal official who served the queen. He had gone to Jerusalem to worship, and on his way home he was sitting in his chariot reading the Book of Isaiah the prophet. The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.”

Philip ran up and heard the man reading Isaiah. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. The passage said that he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation he was deprived of justice, and his life was taken from the earth. The official asked, “Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.

As they traveled along the road, they came to some water, and the official said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” He gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both of them went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the official did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and traveled about, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.
God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. Next week we will see that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. We will meet Saul on the road.
weeks.enochLine: God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus!
enochActivities: Activity: Go! Take a few steps as if you are heading down a road, and say: God can send me to help!
Activity: Open the good news. Open your hands like a book, then point to Jesus, and say: This good news is about Jesus!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 8:26–29, who told Philip to go to the desert road, and who told him to go to the chariot?
In Acts 8:30–31, what did Philip ask, and what did the official say he needed?
In Acts 8:35, what did Philip tell the official, beginning with the passage from Isaiah?
In Acts 8:36, 38–39, what did the official ask when they came to water, and what happened after he was baptized?
elijahAnswers: An angel of the Lord told Philip to go south to the desert road, and the Spirit told him, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” (Acts 8:26, 29).
Philip asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” (Acts 8:30–31).
Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:35).

He said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” Philip baptized him, the Spirit of the Lord took Philip away, and the official went on his way rejoicing (Acts 8:36, 38–39).
jordynQuestions: The official had already gone to Jerusalem to worship and was already reading Isaiah (Acts 8:27–28, 32–34). Why did he still need Philip?

Philip does not start with his own ideas. He begins with that very passage of Scripture and tells the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:35). What does that teach you about helping someone understand the Bible?
This week God sent Philip down a desert road. Next week we will see Saul, who had fought against Jesus, meet him. What do both stories show you about how far the good news is going?
jordynAnswers: Wanting to worship and even reading Scripture is not the same as understanding the good news about Jesus. He asked who the prophet was talking about, and he needed someone to explain it. God sent Philip for that very help.

Start where they are in the word, and show them Jesus. The passage was already about the one whose life was taken, and Philip used it to tell the good news. We do not have to invent a new message. We help people see Jesus in the Scriptures.

God is sending the good news to people who are searching, and he can also go after people who have been fighting him. Philip helps a worshiper from Ethiopia understand. Next week we will see that Jesus can change anyone, even Saul.
weeks.jordynApplication: God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus (Acts 8:26–40). This week, be ready to help someone understand a bit of Scripture, or to tell the good news about Jesus. Next week we will see that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she had a chance to help someone understand the Bible, or to speak the good news about Jesus. If it is fitting, thank God together that he still sends people to explain, and that the official went on his way rejoicing.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that you sent Philip to the desert road to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. Thank you that the Scriptures point to him, and that the official went on his way rejoicing. Make us ready to go where you send us, and to explain the good news with care. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: God sends Philip to a desert road, and to a chariot, to help a man understand.
dailies.verse: How can I, unless someone explains it to me?
dailies.enoch: Take a few steps and say: God can send me to help!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:26–29, where did the angel tell Philip to go, and what did the Spirit tell him when he got there?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The angel told him to go south to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. The Spirit told him, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.”
dailies.jordyn: The official was already reading Isaiah (Acts 8:28, 30). Why is Philip’s question, “Do you understand what you are reading?” such a kind and needed question?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Reading is not the same as understanding. The official was a worshiper and a serious reader, and he still needed someone to explain the Scriptures. God sent Philip to sit with him and help.
dailies.action: Read Acts 8:26–31 together, then tell someone: The official said he needed someone to explain what he was reading.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for sending Philip to the chariot. Give us listening hearts, and make us ready to help someone understand your word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: An angel of the Lord sent Philip south to the desert road. There he met an important official from Ethiopia, who had gone to Jerusalem to worship and was reading Isaiah in his chariot. The Spirit said, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” Philip ran up and asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” Then he invited Philip to sit with him.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up walk a few steps with you, then sit down as if in a chariot, and say: Please help me understand!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:27, who was this official, and what had he gone to Jerusalem to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He was an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake, queen of the Ethiopians, and he had gone to Jerusalem to worship.
dailies.jordyn2: God sent Philip one step at a time: first the road, then the chariot (Acts 8:26, 29). What does that teach you about following the Lord when you do not know the whole plan yet?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Philip started out when he was sent, and then he was told the next step. We do not have to see the whole story before we obey. God can lead us to the person who needs help understanding Jesus.
dailies.passageText: 26 Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” 27 So he started out, and on his way he met an Ethiopian eunuch, an important official in charge of all the treasury of the Kandake (which means “queen of the Ethiopians”). This man had gone to Jerusalem to worship, 28 and on his way home was sitting in his chariot reading the Book of Isaiah the prophet. 29 The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” 30 Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Practice going where you are sent, and helping someone understand the good news.
dailies.verse: The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.”
dailies.enoch: Point down an imaginary road and say: I can go and help!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:30, what did Philip do when he was told to go to the chariot?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet.
dailies.jordyn: How should we play a go-and-help game so that we honor this official, and do not make his questions or his job a joke?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We treat him as a real worshiper who wanted to understand. We practice running to help, listening, and explaining the good news with care, not pretending to mock anyone or make a show of the chariot.
dailies.action: Play a go-and-help game: one person sits with an open Bible, another is sent, runs (or walks quickly) to sit beside them, and says, I can help you understand the good news about Jesus. Then switch.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Philip ran to the chariot to help. Send us with the same willing feet, and teach us to help with respect and joy. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Spirit told Philip to go to the chariot and stay near it. Philip ran up, heard the official reading, and asked if he understood. The official said he could not understand unless someone explained it, and he invited Philip to sit with him. Today we practice that kind of help: going when we are sent, and sitting close enough to explain.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up pretend to send you a few steps, then sit beside them and say: I can help you understand Jesus!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:31, what did the official do after he said he needed someone to explain?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He invited Philip to come up and sit with him.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is sitting with someone a better picture of Philip’s work than shouting the answer from far away?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The official invited him up. Help happened close, with the Scriptures open, in a real conversation. God sent Philip not only to the road, but near the chariot, to stay and explain.
dailies.passageText: 29 The Spirit told Philip, “Go to that chariot and stay near it.” 30 Then Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading Isaiah the prophet. “Do you understand what you are reading?” Philip asked. 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him.

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Philip begins with the Scriptures the official is already reading, and tells him the good news about Jesus.
dailies.verse: Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands like a book and say: This is about Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:32–34, what was the official reading about, and what did he ask Philip?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He was reading about one who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, whose life was taken from the earth. He asked who the prophet was talking about, himself or someone else.
dailies.jordyn: The passage is about someone silent, treated unjustly, whose life is taken (Acts 8:32–33). Why is it such good news that Philip can start there and tell him about Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The Scriptures were already pointing to Jesus, the one who was led like a lamb and whose life was taken for us. Philip does not have to change the subject. He begins with that very passage and tells the good news.
dailies.action: Read Acts 8:32–35 together, then tell someone: Philip started with Isaiah and told the good news about Jesus.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that the Scriptures point to Jesus. Teach us to begin with your word and to tell the good news about him with clear, glad hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The official was reading about one who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, silent as a lamb, deprived of justice, his life taken from the earth. He asked who the prophet was talking about. Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up point from an open Bible to the name of Jesus, and say: The good news is about Jesus!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:35, where did Philip begin his explanation?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He began with that very passage of Scripture the official was already reading.
dailies.jordyn2: Why does “that very passage” matter, instead of Philip starting somewhere easier or more familiar to himself?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He honored the word already open in front of them, and he honored the official’s question. Help that stays with the Scripture in hand can lead a person to Jesus, not just to our favorite verses.
dailies.passageText: 32 This is the passage of Scripture the eunuch was reading: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth. 33 In his humiliation he was deprived of justice. Who can speak of his descendants? For his life was taken from the earth.” 34 The eunuch asked Philip, “Tell me, please, who is the prophet talking about, himself or someone else?” 35 Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Be ready to help someone understand the good news about Jesus this week.
dailies.verse: Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?
dailies.enoch: Open your hands and say: I want to follow Jesus too!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:36 and 38, what did the official want to do when they came to water, and what did they do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He asked what could stand in the way of his being baptized. He gave orders to stop the chariot, and both of them went down into the water, and Philip baptized him.
dailies.jordyn: The official heard the good news, understood, and wanted to be baptized at once (Acts 8:35–38). What would it look like for you to help someone understand the good news this week, at the size of your life?
dailies.jordynAnswer: You might sit with a brother or sister and explain a verse, tell a friend that the good news is about Jesus, or ask a parent to help you practice the story. The challenge is not to be Philip on a desert road overnight. It is to be ready to help someone understand.
dailies.action: Choose one person this week to help with a verse or the good news about Jesus — a sibling, a friend, or someone in your family — and then do it with care.
dailies.prayer: Father, make us ready, like Philip, to help someone understand the good news about Jesus. Give us a glad yes when you send us, and give others open hearts. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Philip told him the good news about Jesus. As they traveled, they came to some water, and the official said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” He stopped the chariot, and Philip baptized him. When God helps someone understand, they may be ready to follow Jesus right away.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up name one person you can tell about Jesus this week, and say: I can help them understand.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:38, who went down into the water?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Both Philip and the official went down into the water, and Philip baptized him.
dailies.jordyn2: The official asks what can stand in the way. Why is that a good question after hearing the good news about Jesus?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: He is not stalling. He has understood, and he wants to belong to Jesus now. When the good news is clear, the next step can be a glad, unhindered yes.
dailies.passageText: 35 Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. 36 As they traveled along the road, they came to some water and the eunuch said, “Look, here is water. What can stand in the way of my being baptized?” 38 And he gave orders to stop the chariot. Then both Philip and the eunuch went down into the water and Philip baptized him.

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God for sending help to understand, and ask to be ready like Philip.
dailies.verse: The eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing.
dailies.enoch: Clap once and say: Thank you, God, for the good news!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:39–40, what happened to Philip, and how did the official go on his way?
dailies.elijahAnswer: The Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away. The official did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and traveled about, preaching the gospel.
dailies.jordyn: The official goes on rejoicing even after Philip is taken away (Acts 8:39). What does that tell you about who the good news depends on?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Philip was a gift, and then the official’s joy did not depend on keeping Philip beside him. The good news is about Jesus. We can thank God for the people who explain, and we can rejoice in Jesus himself.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank God for someone who has helped you understand the Bible, and ask him to make you ready to help someone else.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you for sending people to help us understand the good news about Jesus. Fill us with the official’s joy, and make us ready, like Philip, to go where you send us. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord took Philip away, and the official went on his way rejoicing. Philip appeared at Azotus and kept preaching the gospel in the towns. God can send a helper, give understanding, and then keep both people in his care.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud for one person who has helped you understand Jesus.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:39, who took Philip away?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away.
dailies.jordyn2: Philip keeps preaching after he is taken to Azotus (Acts 8:40). How does that fit with a week about being sent?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The same Lord who sent him to one chariot also sends him on to other towns. Being sent is not a one-time errand. God keeps giving him the good news to preach, and the official keeps going with joy.
dailies.passageText: 39 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing. 40 Philip, however, appeared at Azotus and traveled about, preaching the gospel in all the towns until he reached Caesarea.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus, and next we will see Saul meet Jesus.
dailies.verse: Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus.
dailies.enoch: Take a step, then open your hands, and say: God sends help so we can understand Jesus!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 8:31 and 8:35, what did the official need, and what did Philip give him?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He needed someone to explain the Scriptures, and Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus.
dailies.jordyn: This week God sent Philip down a desert road to help a worshiper understand Jesus. How does that get your heart ready for next week, when we will see Saul, who fought against Jesus, meet him on a road?
dailies.jordynAnswer: God sends the good news both to people who are searching and to people who have been fighting him. Philip helped a man understand. Next week we will see that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. Then thank God, and look ahead to Saul.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus, and that the official went on his way rejoicing. Get our hearts ready to see that you can change anyone. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that God sent Philip to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. An angel sent him to the desert road, and the Spirit sent him to the chariot. The official asked someone to explain the Scriptures. Philip began with that very passage and told him the good news about Jesus. The official was baptized and went on his way rejoicing. Next week we will see Saul meet Jesus, and we will learn that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look down a hall as if it were a road, and say: Next week we will see Saul meet Jesus!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 8:39, how did the official go on his way after Philip was taken away?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He went on his way rejoicing.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is this week’s picture — God sending help so a man could understand Jesus — a fitting last word before a week about Saul?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: This week we saw God send a helper to a searching official. Next week we will see God stop a man who was going the wrong way. In both stories, Jesus is the one the good news is about, and God comes to people on the road.
dailies.passageText: 26 Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, “Go south to the road—the desert road—that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza.” 31 “How can I,” he said, “unless someone explains it to me?” So he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. 35 Then Philip began with that very passage of Scripture and told him the good news about Jesus. 39 When they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly took Philip away, and the eunuch did not see him again, but went on his way rejoicing.

readings.text: 1 Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples. He went to the high priest 2 and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any there who belonged to the Way, whether men or women, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem. 3 As he neared Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” 5 “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. 6 “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” 7 The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless; they heard the sound but did not see anyone. 8 Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus. 9 For three days he was blind, and did not eat or drink anything.

10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. 11 The Lord told him, “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying. 12 In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” 13 “Lord,” Ananias answered, “I have heard many reports about this man and all the harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem. 14 And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on your name.” 15 But the Lord said to Ananias, “Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.”

17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.

story: Last week God sent Philip down a desert road to help a man understand the good news about Jesus. Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples. He went to the high priest and asked for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, whether men or women, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

As he neared Damascus, a light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless. They heard the sound but did not see anyone. Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus. For three days he was blind, and did not eat or drink anything.

In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. The Lord told him to go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying, and in a vision has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight. Ananias answered that he had heard many reports about this man and all the harm he had done to the Lord’s people, and that Saul had come to take prisoners. But the Lord said, “Go!” This man is his chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. The Lord would also show Saul how much he must suffer for the name.

Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, and after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.
Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Next week we will see that the good news of Jesus is for every nation and people. We will meet Peter, and a man named Cornelius.
weeks.enochLine: Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him!
enochActivities: Activity: Bright light. Open your hands like a flash of light, then listen, and say: Jesus can change anyone!
Activity: Brother. Hold out a hand as if to welcome, and say: Ananias called him Brother Saul!
elijahQuestions: In Acts 9:1–2, what was Saul doing as he went to Damascus?
In Acts 9:3–5, what happened as Saul neared Damascus, and what did the voice say?
In Acts 9:10–15, why was Ananias afraid, and what did the Lord tell him about Saul?
In Acts 9:17–19, what did Ananias call Saul, and what happened after he placed his hands on him?
elijahAnswers: Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples, and he asked for letters so that if he found any who belonged to the Way, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem (Acts 9:1–2).

A light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice say, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Saul asked, “Who are you, Lord?” and the voice said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied (Acts 9:3–5).
Ananias had heard many reports about the harm Saul had done, and that he had come to take prisoners. The Lord said, “Go!” This man is his chosen instrument to proclaim his name (Acts 9:13–15).

Ananias said, “Brother Saul,” and told him that the Lord Jesus had sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit. Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, he could see, he was baptized, he ate, and he regained his strength (Acts 9:17–19).
jordynQuestions: Jesus does not only ask why Saul is hurting people. He says, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” (Acts 9:4–5). What does that tell you about how Jesus sees his people?
Ananias was honestly afraid, and still he went and said, “Brother Saul” (Acts 9:13–17). What does that teach you about obeying Jesus when someone has a hard past?
This week Jesus stops a man who fought against him. Next week we will see that the good news is for every nation and people. What do both stories show you about how wide Jesus’ work is?
jordynAnswers: To fight the Lord’s disciples is to fight Jesus himself. Saul thought he was only going after people in Damascus. Jesus says, you are persecuting me. He is that close to his people.

Fear can be real, and Jesus still sends us. Ananias does not pretend Saul’s harm never happened, and he still goes, and he calls him brother. Jesus can change a person so deeply that the church can welcome him.

Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him, and his good news is not for one kind of people only. He stops Saul on the road, and next week we will see him send the good news still farther, to every nation.
weeks.jordynApplication: Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him (Acts 9:1–19). This week, pray for someone who seems far from Jesus, or take one brave step to welcome a person the way Ananias finally went to Saul. Next week we will see that the good news of Jesus is for every nation and people.
weeks.applicationCheck: Ask her later in the week whether she prayed for someone who seems far from Jesus, or whether she had a chance to welcome someone with care. If it is fitting, thank God together that Jesus can change anyone, and that Ananias was willing to go.
weeks.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus met Saul on the road, and that he can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Thank you that Ananias went and called him brother. Make us ready to obey when you send us, and teach us to hope for people who seem far away. In Jesus’ name, Amen.

dailies.label: Day 2 · Passage
dailies.focus: Jesus meets Saul on the road, and names himself as the one Saul has been fighting.
dailies.verse: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands like a flash of light, then listen, and say: Jesus can change anyone!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:3–6, what did Saul see and hear on the road, and what was he told to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: A light from heaven flashed around him. He fell and heard, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” Then, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” He was told, “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.”
dailies.jordyn: Saul thought he was only going after disciples (Acts 9:1–2). Why does it matter that Jesus says, “why do you persecute me?”
dailies.jordynAnswer: Jesus stands with his people so closely that to hurt them is to hurt him. Saul meets the Lord himself, not only a new idea about religion.
dailies.action: Read Acts 9:1–9 together, then tell someone: On the road, Jesus told Saul, I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus met Saul on the road and told him the truth. Meet us too, and change hearts that have been fighting you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Saul was on his way to Damascus to take followers of Jesus as prisoners. A light from heaven flashed around him. He fell to the ground and heard a voice: “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” “Who are you, Lord?” “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. Saul was led into the city, blind, and for three days he did not eat or drink.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up listen quietly for a moment, then say: Jesus called Saul by name!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:8–9, what happened to Saul after he got up from the ground?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: When he opened his eyes he could see nothing. The men with him led him by the hand into Damascus, and for three days he was blind and did not eat or drink anything.
dailies.jordyn2: For three days Saul is blind, and he does not eat or drink (Acts 9:9). What might those days be teaching him, before Ananias even arrives?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The man who had been so sure is stopped and has to wait. Jesus has already spoken, and Saul cannot hurry on in his old way. Waiting can be part of being changed.
dailies.passageText: 1 Meanwhile, Saul was still breathing out murderous threats against the Lord’s disciples. He went to the high priest 2 and asked him for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that if he found any there who belonged to the Way, whether men or women, he might take them as prisoners to Jerusalem. 3 As he neared Damascus on his journey, suddenly a light from heaven flashed around him. 4 He fell to the ground and heard a voice say to him, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” 5 “Who are you, Lord?” Saul asked. “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” he replied. 6 “Now get up and go into the city, and you will be told what you must do.” 7 The men traveling with Saul stood there speechless; they heard the sound but did not see anyone. 8 Saul got up from the ground, but when he opened his eyes he could see nothing. So they led him by the hand into Damascus. 9 For three days he was blind, and did not eat or drink anything.

dailies.label: Day 3 · Game
dailies.focus: Practice a willing yes, and a kind welcome, like Ananias going to Saul.
dailies.verse: Yes, Lord.
dailies.enoch: Hold out a hand and say: Yes, Lord. I can go and welcome!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:10, what did Ananias say when the Lord called his name?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He answered, “Yes, Lord,”
dailies.jordyn: How should we play a yes-and-welcome game so that we honor this story, and do not make Saul’s blindness or his threats into a joke?
dailies.jordynAnswer: We do not pretend to be blind, and we do not act out harm. We practice Ananias’s yes, and the kind words Brother Saul, because Jesus can change a person and then send us to welcome him.
dailies.action: Play a yes-and-welcome game: one person says a simple send, like, Please go to your brother, and the other answers, Yes, Lord, walks over, and says, Brother, Jesus can change anyone. Then switch.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Ananias said, “Yes, Lord,” and then called Saul brother. Give us a willing yes, and a kind welcome for people you are changing. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Lord called Ananias in a vision, and Ananias answered, “Yes, Lord,” Later he went into the house, placed his hands on Saul, and said, “Brother Saul,” Today we practice those two words: a willing yes, and a kind welcome, because Jesus can change anyone.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up call your name softly. Answer, Yes, Lord, then hold out a welcome hand.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:17, what name did Ananias use for the man who had come to arrest believers?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He said, “Brother Saul,”
dailies.jordyn2: Why is Brother Saul a better line to practice than trying to act out the light or the blindness?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The miracle belongs to Jesus. Our part, like Ananias, is to go when we are sent and to welcome the person Jesus is changing. The welcome is the part we can practice with honor.
dailies.passageText: 10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. 17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

dailies.label: Day 4 · Passage
dailies.focus: Ananias goes, calls Saul brother, and Saul can see again.
dailies.verse: Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus… has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.
dailies.enoch: Hold out a welcome hand and say: Brother Saul! Jesus can change anyone!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:13–17, what was Ananias afraid of, and what did he do anyway?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He had heard about the harm Saul had done, and that Saul had come to take prisoners. The Lord said, “Go!” and Ananias went, placed his hands on Saul, and called him “Brother Saul,”
dailies.jordyn: The Lord does not deny Saul’s harm, and still he sends Ananias and calls Saul his chosen instrument (Acts 9:13–15). How does that hold truth and mercy together?
dailies.jordynAnswer: The past is not pretended away. Jesus still chooses Saul and sends him. Mercy does not mean the harm never happened. It means Jesus is strong enough to change a person and then use him.
dailies.action: Read Acts 9:10–19 together, then tell someone: Ananias went and said, Brother Saul.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that you sent Ananias, and that Saul could see again and was baptized. Give us courage to go to people you are changing. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: The Lord sent Ananias to Saul, even though Ananias was afraid. “Go!” the Lord said. This man is his chosen instrument to proclaim his name. Ananias went, placed his hands on him, and said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes. He could see, he was baptized, he ate, and he regained his strength.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up place a gentle hand on your shoulder, like a kind welcome, and say: Jesus can help us see!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:18–19, what happened after Ananias placed his hands on Saul?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, and after taking some food, he regained his strength.
dailies.jordyn2: Saul spends several days with the disciples in Damascus (Acts 9:19). Why is that a fitting end to this week’s official passage?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: The man who came to arrest them now stays with them. Jesus does not only stop Saul on the road. He brings him into the family, starting with Ananias’s words, “Brother Saul,”
dailies.passageText: 10 In Damascus there was a disciple named Ananias. The Lord called to him in a vision, “Ananias!” “Yes, Lord,” he answered. 11 The Lord told him, “Go to the house of Judas on Straight Street and ask for a man from Tarsus named Saul, for he is praying. 12 In a vision he has seen a man named Ananias come and place his hands on him to restore his sight.” 13 “Lord,” Ananias answered, “I have heard many reports about this man and all the harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem. 14 And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on your name.” 15 But the Lord said to Ananias, “Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” 17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.

dailies.label: Day 5 · Challenge
dailies.focus: Pray for someone who seems far from Jesus, or take one brave welcome step this week.
dailies.verse: Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name.
dailies.enoch: Hold out both hands and say: Jesus, please change people who still fight you!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:15, what did the Lord say Saul was chosen to do?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He is the Lord’s chosen instrument to proclaim his name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel.
dailies.jordyn: Ananias had to go to someone he was afraid of (Acts 9:13–17). What would a right-sized challenge look like for you this week?
dailies.jordynAnswer: You might pray by name for someone who seems far from Jesus, or take one kind step toward a person who is hard to like. The challenge is not to fix anyone. It is to believe that Jesus can change anyone, and to be willing, like Ananias, to go.
dailies.action: Choose one person this week who seems far from Jesus, or hard to welcome. Pray for them by name, and if you can, take one kind step toward them.
dailies.prayer: Father, you sent Ananias to a man he feared, because Jesus can change anyone. Give us names to pray, and give us courage to go. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Ananias told the Lord what he had heard about Saul’s harm. The Lord still said, “Go!” Saul was his chosen instrument. Ananias went and called him “Brother Saul,” Jesus can change anyone, and he often sends someone willing to walk toward that person.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up name one person you can pray for this week, and say their name in a short prayer.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:17, who sent Ananias to Saul?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: The Lord Jesus, who appeared to Saul on the road, sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is prayer a fitting first step, even if you cannot go to someone the way Ananias did?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: Ananias started with the Lord, too, in a vision and a conversation. We can bring a name to Jesus first. He is the one who changes people, and he can also show us if there is a next step to take.
dailies.passageText: 13 “Lord,” Ananias answered, “I have heard many reports about this man and all the harm he has done to your holy people in Jerusalem. 14 And he has come here with authority from the chief priests to arrest all who call on your name.” 15 But the Lord said to Ananias, “Go! This man is my chosen instrument to proclaim my name to the Gentiles and their kings and to the people of Israel. 16 I will show him how much he must suffer for my name.” 17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”

dailies.label: Day 6 · Prayer
dailies.focus: Thank God that Jesus can change anyone, and ask for Ananias’s willing heart.
dailies.verse: Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again.
dailies.enoch: Open your eyes wide and say: Thank you, Jesus, for changing Saul!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:18–19, what did Saul do after he could see again?
dailies.elijahAnswer: He got up and was baptized, and after taking some food, he regained his strength. He spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.
dailies.jordyn: Saul is baptized and then stays with the disciples (Acts 9:18–19). What does that tell you to thank God for, besides the flash of light on the road?
dailies.jordynAnswer: Thank God that change leads into a new family, not only a moment on the road. Saul can see, he is baptized, he is fed, and he is with the disciples. Jesus gives a whole new life, not just a stopped plan.
dailies.action: Pray together: thank God that Jesus changed Saul, and ask him to give you a willing heart like Ananias, and hope for people who still seem far away.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Thank you for scales falling, for baptism, and for a place with the disciples. Give us Ananias’s yes, and fill us with hope. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: Ananias called him “Brother Saul,” and the Lord Jesus filled him with the Holy Spirit. Something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes. He could see, he was baptized, he ate, and he stayed with the disciples. This is a story for thanking God, and for asking him to keep changing people.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up thank God out loud that Jesus can change anyone.
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:19, who did Saul spend several days with?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: He spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.
dailies.jordyn2: How does praying this story keep both the miracle and the welcome in view?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: We thank God for the light, the voice, and the scales. We also thank him that a frightened disciple said, “Brother Saul,” and that Saul was then at the table with the very people he had come to harm. Both parts are gifts.
dailies.passageText: 17 Then Ananias went to the house and entered it. Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 18 Immediately, something like scales fell from Saul’s eyes, and he could see again. He got up and was baptized, 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.

dailies.label: Day 7 · Recap
dailies.focus: Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him, and next we will see good news for every nation.
dailies.verse: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting.
dailies.enoch: Open your hands like a light, then hold out a welcome hand, and say: Jesus can change anyone!
dailies.elijah: In Acts 9:5 and 9:17, what did Jesus say on the road, and what did Ananias say in the house?
dailies.elijahAnswer: Jesus said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” Ananias said, “Brother Saul,” and told him that the Lord Jesus had sent him so that Saul might see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.
dailies.jordyn: This week Jesus stopped a man who fought against him and made him a brother. How does that get your heart ready for next week, when we will see that the good news is for every nation and people?
dailies.jordynAnswer: If Jesus can change Saul, he can also send the good news farther than we expected. Next week we will meet Peter and a man named Cornelius, and we will learn that the good news of Jesus is for every nation and people.
dailies.action: Tell someone the week’s big idea: Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Then thank God, and look ahead to Peter and Cornelius.
dailies.prayer: Father, thank you that Jesus met Saul on the road and can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Get our hearts ready to see that your good news is for every nation and people. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
dailies.teach: This week we learned that Jesus can change anyone, even someone who fought against him. Saul was on his way to take followers of Jesus as prisoners. A light flashed, and Jesus said, “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting,” Ananias was afraid, and still he went and said, “Brother Saul,” Scales fell, Saul could see, he was baptized, and he stayed with the disciples. Next week we will see that the good news of Jesus is for every nation and people, when we meet Peter and Cornelius.
dailies.enochActivity: Help a grown-up look down a hall as if it were a road, and say: Next week the good news is for every nation!
dailies.elijah2: In Acts 9:19, what did Saul do after he regained his strength?
dailies.elijahAnswer2: Saul spent several days with the disciples in Damascus.
dailies.jordyn2: Why is Jesus can change anyone a fitting last word before a week about every nation?
dailies.jordynAnswer2: This week we saw Jesus stop an enemy and make him a brother. Next week we will see that the same good news is not only for one group of people. The Lord who changes Saul also sends the good news to every nation.

Placing his hands on Saul, he said, “Brother Saul, the Lord—Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here—has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” 19 and after taking some food, he regained his strength. howSteps.detail: Still on Read, walk through the kid-language explanation so everyone gets the picture.
